`CLAUDE.md`:

```md
# CLAUDE.md

Spec-driven development, scaffolded and checked by `scc`. The methodology lives in `.claude/rules/` — never inline it here.

## Rules — `.claude/rules/<name>.md`

Claude Code loads `.claude/rules/` at session start — nothing to open, bar `specs.md`,
`tasks.md` and `knowledge-base.md`, read when you touch their tree. The failure is not a
rule you never read, it is one you had and misapplied — so the triggers say *when* each governs.

`caveman.md` is always on: the register you answer in. The rest, by where you are:

- `autonomy.md` — at kickoff, before writing anything
- `prior-art.md` — then read what `docs/` already decides, before the first artifact
- `routing.md` — work arrives and needs a vehicle: a spec, or a plan
- `methodology.md` — starting a task: which cycle, what to run first
- `ladder.md` — about to write the code: how much of it the task gets
- `verification.md` — code is written and you think it is done
- `delivery.md` — last task done: branch, review, PR

Triggered by what you are about to touch:

- `project.md` — **before any build, test, lint, or format command.** This project's
  commands exist nowhere else; a guessed one that exits 0 looks like a passing suite.
- `code-search.md` — before going looking for code you have not read
- `artifacts.md` — before opening a plan or a spec
- `specs.md` — writing requirements, design, or tasks for a spec
- `tasks.md` — working through a spec's task list
- `knowledge-base.md` — something was learned, or a decision was made
- `notes.md` — **before typing a comment that is not a docstring**; `scc notes find --path <f>`

## Ask the index before you read the file

**Code** — `scc graph query|explore <symbol>`; read the source to change it, not to find it.

**Plans and specs** — a plan is a header and a checklist: `map brief <plan>` once, then
`map tasks <plan> --next` per task; **never open the plan**. Also `scc map` and `map
show <artifact> <address>`. An address is a name, never a line number: `1.2` `#risks`.

**Changing one** — `scc patch check <artifact> 1.2`, plus `task` `add` `append` `fm`. Not
an editor: it resolves the address, re-validates, and rolls back an edit that adds a
finding — so you need not read a plan to change one line of it.

## Layout

```
specs/<feature>/    requirements.md · design.md · tasks.md
plans/<name>.md     structure, plus a checklist and/or spec references
docs/               knowledge base — wiki, adr, codewiki, glossary, stack, notes
.claude/rules/      the methodology above
.claude/skills/     authoring each part of docs/, and running a plan group by group
                    on demand too: /scc-plan-run, /scc-wiki, /scc-adr, …
```

## Checking your work

`scc validate` — or `npx @protonspy/scc validate` if not installed (`@<version>` pins for CI).
`scc update` brings a newer scc's rules and agents in: it shows the plan, then asks.
Exit `0` ok · `1` could not run · `2` ran and found something. A finding is an answer, not a crash.
`scc` checks artifact *shape* only; it never reads source, so whether the code honors it is on you.

<!-- rtk-instructions v2 -->
## RTK
Prefix EVERY command with `rtk`, including each link in a `&&` chain (`rtk git add . && rtk git commit -m "x"`).
No dedicated filter means it passes through unchanged — always safe.

Covered:
- cargo build/check/clippy/test, go test, tsc, lint, prettier, next build
- jest, vitest, playwright, pytest, rspec, rake test, test `<cmd>`
- git (all subcommands)
- gh pr view/checks, gh run list, gh issue list, gh api
- pnpm, npm run, npx, prisma, uv run
- ls, read, grep, find
- err, log, json, deps, env, summary, diff
- docker, kubectl, curl, wget

Meta: `rtk gain [--history]`, `rtk discover`, `rtk proxy <cmd>` (no filtering), `rtk init [--global]`
Caveat: `rtk grep` with `-c -l -L -o -Z` runs raw.
<!-- /rtk-instructions -->

```

# Harness for REA

A desktop app and a terminal UI for deep analysis of software you own or are authorized to study:
understanding a legacy system, debugging, reverse engineering a binary or an app, and porting or
reimplementing what it does.

You describe what you want in a chat. Two agents do the work:

| Agent                | Runs on                                                                    | Does                                                                                                                                       |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **The orchestrator** | a model from OpenRouter, DeepSeek or any OpenAI-compatible provider        | the agent you talk to: plans the task, prepares each step, writes and runs its own code (a decoder, a reimplementation, a probe), answers you |
| **The specialist**   | Claude Opus running the Claude Code CLI on your own Claude plan, in Docker | the deep analysis, in a container holding only the files a step needs, with [REA](https://github.com/morluto/rea) built in and a root shell |

[REA](https://github.com/morluto/rea) is a reverse engineering MCP server for native binaries,
Android, .NET, Electron and JavaScript targets. The orchestrator does not analyse the target itself.

The split keeps the expensive, careful work with the specialist and the cheap planning and coding
with the orchestrator, and keeps the target away from your machine: the specialist only ever sees
copies of the files it was handed.

## How a task runs

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    you(["You"]) <-->|"chat, questions,<br/>patches to approve"| orch["Orchestrator<br/>your provider's model"]
    orch -.-> log[("Event log<br/>SQLite + JSONL")]

    subgraph specc["Specialist container"]
        claude["Specialist<br/>Claude Code"] --- rea["REA"]
        claude --- work["Copies of the<br/>listed files"]
    end

    subgraph taskc["Task container"]
        tools["Orchestrator's tools<br/>workspace read-only<br/>scratch writable"]
    end

    orch -->|"context package"| claude
    claude -.->|"report + evidence<br/>+ contract"| orch
    orch -->|"writes and runs its code,<br/>replays test vectors"| tools
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor You
    participant O as Orchestrator
    participant H as Harness
    participant S as Specialist
    participant T as Task container

    You->>O: Request
    O->>O: Break it into steps
    O->>H: Delegate a step with a context package
    H->>S: Fresh container, files copied into /work
    S->>S: Analyse with REA and a shell
    S-->>H: Report citing evidence, ending with a contract
    H->>H: Validate the contract
    opt The contract fails
        H->>S: Send it back for a correction, up to twice
        S-->>H: Corrected report
    end
    H-->>O: Report and contract
    O->>T: Write its code and run replay_vectors
    T-->>O: Outputs compared byte for byte
    O-->>You: Answer, and a patch to approve
    You->>H: Approve the patch
    H->>H: Apply it to your files
```

1. **You start a task** in a project with a request. The orchestrator breaks it into steps.
2. **For each analysis**, the orchestrator writes a _context package_: a technical brief (what the
   artifact is, what is already known), the objective, the files, the questions and the report
   format. The specialist sees that package and nothing else — not your request, not the chat.
3. **The specialist runs** in a fresh container (or a sandbox the orchestrator prepared with tools
   and files), with the files copied into `/work`. It answers with a report whose claims cite
   evidence: a line range, an address in a binary, or an REA evidence id.
4. **Every report ends with a contract**, a JSON block the app validates: the functions mapped with
   their inputs, outputs and side effects; the constants found, each with a source or marked
   estimated; the questions left open; and _test vectors_ — inputs given to the target and the
   output it produced, observed by running it. A report whose contract fails is sent back to the
   specialist for a correction, up to twice.
5. **The orchestrator writes its code** from the report and checks it with `replay_vectors`, which
   runs the vectors against its reimplementation and compares outputs byte for byte.
6. **Changes to your files** come back as patches. Nothing outside the task's containers changes
   until a patch is applied.

### Questions and refusals

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    q["The specialist asks a question"] --> om{"Can the orchestrator's model<br/>answer it from the context package?"}
    om -- "yes" --> back["The answer goes back to the specialist"]
    om -- "no: only you know" --> user["You are asked"]
    r["The specialist declines a step<br/>under its usage policy"] --> wait["The task waits for you"]
    wait --> stop["Stop the task"]
    wait --> skip["Skip the step"]
    wait --> other["Ask for a different<br/>technical approach"]
```

**Questions.** Either agent can ask you a question mid-run. The specialist's questions go first to
the orchestrator's model, which answers from the context package when it can; questions about
authorization, ownership or purpose always come to you.

**Refusals.** If the specialist declines a step under its usage policy, the task waits for you to
stop it, skip the step, or ask for a different technical approach. The request is never reworded to
get past the refusal.

**Projects.** A project is one target — a file (an APK, an executable, an archive) or a folder —
with a goal and the model its tasks use. Tasks in a project share its sandboxes and everything
earlier tasks found, and the questions one analysis left open are handed to the next.

## Isolation

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph host["Your machine"]
        files["Your files"]
        keys["OS keychain<br/>one entry per provider"]
        data[("App data folder<br/>event log + raw output")]
        app["Harness for REA"]

        subgraph docker["Docker"]
            taskc["Task container<br/>your source read-only,<br/>scratch area, internet"]
            specc["Specialist container<br/>copies of your files,<br/>as root, internet"]
            vol[("Volume<br/>Claude sign-in token")]
        end
    end

    files -- "mounted read-only" --> taskc
    files -- "copied" --> specc
    vol -- "mounted" --> specc
    keys --> app
    app --> data
    app -. "patch, on your approval" .-> files
```

- The specialist runs in a container per delegation, or in a sandbox the orchestrator created for
  the project; of your files it sees only the copies made for it, as root, with internet access.
  Its Claude Code runs with no user or project settings, so a `CLAUDE.md` or settings left in
  `/work` by an earlier step are never loaded.
- The orchestrator's tools run in a task container, as root with internet access, where your
  source is mounted read-only; they write to your machine only through its scratch area.
- The specialist signs in with your Claude plan once; the token lives in a Docker volume mounted
  into the specialist's container.

> [!WARNING]
> The container keeps a target away from your machine, not from your Claude account. The specialist
> has a root shell and internet access beside the sign-in token, so a hostile target that steers it
> can read the token and send it out. Do not analyse an untrusted sample with an account you cannot
> afford to expose.
- Provider API keys are kept in the OS keychain, in one entry per provider both apps read, and
  redacted from everything the app records or sends to a model.
- Everything the agents do is recorded per task: an event log in SQLite and each agent's raw output
  as JSONL, in the app's data folder.

## MCP integrations

Engines that run on your machine reach the agents only through the app. **Cheat Engine** is the
first: the agents read the live memory of a Windows process you approved, through a bridge the app
ships and that answers read-only commands only.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph specc["Specialist container"]
        cc["Claude Code"] --> mcp["MCP server<br/>the tools you allowed"]
    end
    orch["Orchestrator"]

    subgraph host["Your machine"]
        app{"Harness for REA<br/>checks the agent,<br/>the tool and the target"}
        ce["Cheat Engine<br/>+ read-only bridge"]
        proc["The approved process"]
    end

    mcp -- "calls over the run directory" --> app
    orch -- "its allowed tools" --> app
    app --> ce
    ce -- "reads memory" --> proc
```

- **Settings → MCP integrations** lists the integrations the app carries, each off by default. Turning one on
  runs its checks — for Cheat Engine: the executable exists, the bridge script is installed in its
  `autorun` folder, and the bridge answers with the version the app carries — and a failed check
  says what fixes it.
- **Each integration has its own page**, with one toggle per tool for the orchestrator and one for
  the specialist. The specialist starts with every tool; the orchestrator starts with `status` and
  `get_process_list` only, and turning on a tool that reads a target warns that what it returns
  goes to the orchestrator's provider.
- **Every target is approved by you**, shown by its name, PID and executable path, even in an
  automatic task. A delegation with an approved process cannot reach any other. What the tools
  read from it — secrets included — goes to the agents' models and their reports, and the
  specialist's container has full internet access.
- **The bridge only reads**: the process list, modules, memory regions, memory, value and byte
  scans, pointer chains, disassembly, symbols and structures. Writing memory, injecting code and
  debugging are not there to call. Its pipe takes any local client, so while Cheat Engine runs
  with the bridge, the app's checks bind the agents but not other programs on your machine.
- **The container gets nothing new**: no mount, port or environment variable. Each call is
  recorded in the task's event log with its agent, tool, target and outcome, never its answer.

Integrations are set up in the desktop app; the terminal UI uses them as Settings has them.

## What you need

- **Docker** (Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS), running. At the first start the app pulls the
  specialist's base image from GHCR and builds the specialist image on it.
- **A Claude plan** (Pro or Max) for the specialist.
- **An API key** for the orchestrator's provider: OpenRouter by default, DeepSeek, or any
  OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
- **Cheat Engine** on Windows, only for its integration.

## Install

Download the build for your system from the
[releases](https://github.com/protonspy/harness-for-rea/releases):

| System                      | Desktop app                                       | Terminal UI                                        |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Windows x64                 | `harness-for-rea-<version>-windows-x64-setup.exe` | `harness-for-rea-cli-<version>-windows-x64.zip`    |
| macOS arm64 (Apple silicon) | `harness-for-rea-<version>-macos-arm64.dmg`       | `harness-for-rea-cli-<version>-macos-arm64.tar.gz` |
| macOS x64 (Intel)           | `harness-for-rea-<version>-macos-x64.dmg`         | `harness-for-rea-cli-<version>-macos-x64.tar.gz`   |

Nothing is signed or notarized, so each system asks once:

- **Windows** — SmartScreen may stop the setup: choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**.
- **macOS, the desktop app** — drag it from the disk image to Applications, then, before the first
  launch, run:

  ```bash
  xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Harness for REA.app"
  ```

- **macOS, the terminal UI** — unpack the archive, then run in its folder:

  ```bash
  xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ./harness-for-rea
  ./harness-for-rea
  ```

  Keep the `sandbox/` folder next to the binary: it holds the specialist image's sources and the
  MCP integrations' files.

The terminal UI is also on npm, for Windows and macOS:

```bash
npm install -g harness-for-rea
cd path/to/what/you/analyse
harness-for-rea
```

## First run

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    images["1 · Sandbox images<br/>Docker running,<br/>specialist image prepared"] --> login["2 · Claude sign-in<br/>in a container,<br/>with your Claude plan"]
    login --> orch["3 · Orchestrator<br/>provider, API key,<br/>model"]
    orch --> ready(["Ready"])
```

Both apps open on a setup of three steps, and nothing else opens until all three are ready:

1. **Sandbox images** — Docker running and the specialist image prepared.
2. **Claude sign-in** — runs in a container: open the link it shows, sign in with your Claude plan,
   and paste the code back.
3. **Orchestrator** — the provider, its API key and the model.

In the terminal UI the setup opens inline and each step is a command: `/images` prepares the
images again, `/login` opens the sign-in in your browser and `/code <code>` sends the code back,
`/provider`, `/base-url <url>`, `/key <key>` and `/model` (a list to pick from) set the
orchestrator, and `/done` finishes once every step is ready. A step readied in either app is ready
in the other.

## Using it

**Desktop app.** Create a project from a target and a goal, then start tasks in it. A task shows as
a chat: the messages, each tool call, and each delegation as a card with the specialist's own steps
inside it. Long tasks load their history in pages as you scroll up. The side panel has the plan,
the delegations with their reports and evidence, the cost per agent, and the raw event log. The
project page lists its tasks, what the specialist found, and the questions still open. Settings is
split into tabs: Orchestrator model, Sandbox, Specialist, MCP integrations and You in the loop.

**Terminal UI.** Run `harness-for-rea` in the folder you want to analyse, or give its path:
`harness-for-rea C:\samples\app`. The folder is the target of the project it opens — the one
project on it, a choice when there are several, or a new one prefilled with the folder's name, its
detected kind and your Settings model. A home folder, a drive, a Downloads folder or one holding the
app's data asks you to type its path before it is mounted; the app's data folder itself is refused.
`--continue` reopens the folder's last task and `--resume` lists its tasks.

A task is a conversation: the agent's messages as markdown with colored code, each tool call on one
line with its arguments and output under it, each delegation with its context package, report,
evidence, files and the specialist's own steps, and a working line with the elapsed time, tokens and
cost. Questions and gated tool calls open as dialogs; a proposed patch shows as a diff. The sidebar
has the plan, the delegations, the cost per agent and the files touched.

| Key    | Does                                                               |
| ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Enter  | send the message; Shift+Enter or Ctrl+J starts a new line          |
| ↑ ↓    | the messages sent this session, at the prompt's first and last line |
| `/`    | the screen's commands, completed with Tab                          |
| `@`    | a path from the project's folder, completed with Tab               |
| Ctrl+P | every command, searchable                                          |
| Tab    | move between the prompt and the transcript or list                 |
| Ctrl+O | expand or collapse every tool call and delegation                  |
| Ctrl+B | show or hide the sidebar                                           |
| Esc    | stop the running turn, close a dialog, or go back                  |
| Ctrl+C | clear the prompt; twice to quit                                    |
| `?`    | every key on the screen                                            |

Commands on a task: `/stop`, `/continue`, `/close`, `/cancel`, `/start-over`, `/delete`, `/answer`,
`/decide`, `/approve-patch`, `/reject-patch`, `/events` (the event log, filtered by agent) and
`/older`. Everywhere: `/projects`, `/tasks`, `/new`, `/settings`, `/setup`, `/sidebar`, `/quit`.
`--theme light` (or `HFR_THEME=light`) switches to the light colors.

**Side by side.** Any number of terminal UIs, each in its own folder, run beside the desktop app on
the same data folder. A project runs its tasks in one app at a time: while one app runs a task of
it, the others show it as taken and can read its tasks but not start one there. An app that stops
leaves the others' tasks alone; the next app to start recovers what it was running. A key saved in
one app is used by the others. `harness-for-rea --version` and `--help` work at any time.

## How the code is organized

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    desktop["Desktop app<br/>Electron, React, shadcn/ui"] -- "IPC" --> dispatch
    tui["Terminal UI<br/>OpenTUI on Bun"] -- "in process" --> dispatch
    dispatch{"Validating dispatcher<br/>zod schemas"} --> core["startCore()"]
    core --> events[("Event log<br/>SQLite + JSONL")]
    core --> runner["Task runner<br/>and orchestrator"]
    core --> integrations["MCP integrations"]
    runner --> delegation["Delegations"]
    delegation --> docker["Docker<br/>task and specialist containers"]
    integrations --> delegation
```

```
src/main/            the core (Node): Electron shell and everything behind it
  core.ts            wires the database, event log, projects, sandboxes, runner and API handlers
  index.ts           the Electron shell: window, IPC, dialogs
  orchestrator/      the orchestrator agent, its tools, the task runner, the model
  delegation.ts      one delegation: workspace, specialist run, contract check, patch
  specialist/        running Claude Code and reading its stream-json output
  sandbox/           Docker: images, containers, sandboxes, prompts, patches
  integrations/      the MCP integrations: registry, tool gate, target approval, settings
  cheatengine/       Cheat Engine's integration and the pipe to its bridge
  events/            the event log (SQLite + JSONL) and redaction
  unknowns.ts        the per-project ledger of open questions
src/shared/          types and the IPC contract (zod schemas) shared with the views
src/renderer/        the desktop UI (React, Tailwind, shadcn/ui on Radix)
tui/                 the terminal UI (OpenTUI's React layer on Bun) and its npm package
sandbox/             the specialist's images, the integrations' MCP server and Cheat Engine's bridge
scripts/             test gate, image pinning, CLI build
tests/               Vitest suite; the specialist is faked by tests/fixtures/fake-claude.mjs
```

The desktop app and the terminal UI run the same core: `startCore()` takes the data folder, how to
deliver updates to the view, and where keys are kept, and returns the API handlers. Every call from
either UI goes through the same validating dispatcher.

## Development

Node 24 and npm; Docker for the sandboxes; Bun 1.4 for the terminal UI.

```bash
# Install (npm 11 skips install scripts; the Electron binary is fetched by its own script)
npm install
node node_modules/electron/install.js

# Typecheck, then build main, preload and renderer into out/
npm run typecheck && npm run build

# Run the desktop app in development
npm run dev

# Run the terminal UI from source
npm run tui

# Tests: the suite, one file, and the coverage report the CI gate reads
npm test
npx vitest run tests/orchestrator.test.ts
node scripts/test-gate.mjs

# Tests against the real Docker and your Claude login, and against Bun: the core under Bun, and the
# terminal UI's screen tests on OpenTUI's test renderer; the gate counts both with HFR_BUN=1, as CI does
HFR_DOCKER=1 npx vitest run tests/claude-md.test.ts
HFR_BUN=1 npx vitest run tests/bun-core.test.ts
bun test tui/test

# Lint and format
npm run lint
npm run format:check

# Package: Windows installer, macOS disk images, the CLI's npm package and a standalone binary
npm run dist
npm run dist:mac
bun scripts/build-cli.ts package
bun scripts/build-cli.ts binary bun-windows-x64 cli
```

Tests run the TypeScript sources directly. The specialist is `tests/fixtures/fake-claude.mjs`, which
speaks Claude Code's stream-json; the orchestrator's provider is a scripted `fetch`.

### Releasing

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    bump["Bump version<br/>in package.json"] --> run["Run Release<br/>on main"]
    run --> check["check<br/>the tag and npm<br/>version are free"]
    check --> win["windows<br/>installer + CLI"]
    check --> mac["macos<br/>arm64 and x64 images + CLI"]
    win --> pub["publish<br/>GitHub Release, then npm"]
    mac --> pub
```

To release, bump `version` in `package.json` and run the **Release** workflow on `main`. It builds
everything above for Windows and macOS, publishes a GitHub Release, and publishes the CLI to npm
with the `NPM_TOKEN` repository secret.

### Hopper request attribution

When an OpenAI-compatible provider uses `https://api.withhopper.com/v1`, the
app identifies itself with `X-Hopper-Client: harness-for-rea` on model-list,
connection-test and orchestrator requests, including streams. The header contains
only the app name; it adds no user, project or machine identifiers. Other
provider origins receive no Hopper attribution header. Any partner pricing is
controlled by Hopper; this header does not grant access or guarantee a discount.

# 0001 · Use DeepAgents on OpenRouter for orchestration

## Context

The orchestrator plans a task, splits it into steps, decides when a step needs the
specialist, and consolidates the results. The user picks its model, and the app must
not be tied to one vendor, so the model is reached through OpenRouter. The
reference project `study-lab` already runs DeepAgents 1.15.1 on `ChatOpenRouter`
from `@langchain/openrouter` in an Electron main process, with tests driven by a
scripted `fetch`. DeepAgents (JS) provides what the orchestrator would otherwise
build by hand: `write_todos` for decomposition, subagents and custom tools for
delegation, pluggable filesystem backends (`FilesystemBackend`, `CompositeBackend`),
`interruptOn` for approve/edit/reject before a tool runs, and a checkpointer for
resuming a run. The user asked for this framework explicitly.

## Decision

The orchestrator is a `createDeepAgent` agent whose model is a `ChatOpenRouter`
instance configured from the user's settings. The Claude specialist is exposed to it
as a custom tool, not as a DeepAgents subagent, because it runs in its own process
with its own tools and context. Rejected: a hand-written tool-calling loop over the
OpenRouter HTTP API, which `study-lab` also has, because it would re-implement
planning, approval interrupts and checkpointing; and LangGraph directly, which is
the layer DeepAgents already composes.

## Consequences

- Orchestration code is shaped around LangChain message and tool types; replacing
  DeepAgents later means rewriting the orchestrator, not swapping a client.
- `study-lab` needed `legacy-peer-deps` to install DeepAgents beside `langsmith`;
  this project inherits that peer-dependency friction until it is resolved upstream.
- Tools run in the Electron main process; heavy work inside a tool must be moved off
  it or the UI stalls.
- OpenRouter receives source code; requests default to `provider.data_collection:
  "deny"`.
- Model pricing and token usage come from OpenRouter's `usage` object rather than a
  local price list.

```

# 0002 · Run the specialist through the pinned Claude Code CLI

## Context

The specialist is Claude Opus running the Claude Code agent loop. Two integrations
exist: the Claude Agent SDK (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`, which offers
`canUseTool`, `permissionMode` and `cwd` per session), and spawning the `claude` CLI
headless with `--output-format stream-json`. Both reference projects already use the
second, tested: `study-lab` (`src/main/claude/*`, CLI 2.1.310) and the MagnoTech
desktop app (`desktop/electron/turno.ts`, `leitorDoStream.ts`, CLI 2.1.309). Both
download a version pinned by SHA-256, check the Authenticode or codesign signature,
isolate `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, allowlist the environment, force `--setting-sources ""`
and `--strict-mcp-config`, refuse flags that reopen tools, and kill the process tree
with `taskkill /T` on Windows. Each has a fake CLI used by its tests.

## Decision

Port the pinned-CLI executor from `study-lab`, adding from MagnoTech the subagent
attribution and size caps of `leitorDoStream.ts`, multi-turn stdin, and the
loopback hook server. Rejected: the Agent SDK, because adopting it discards two
tested implementations and their fake-CLI harnesses, and its permission callback is
replaceable by `PreToolUse` hooks to the loopback server.

## Consequences

- The app depends on CLI flags and the stream-json event shape of one pinned
  version; upgrading the pin is a deliberate, tested change.
- Unknown event types must be logged and the raw stream kept, or a schema change
  fails silently.
- Each install downloads a binary of roughly 300 MB; Linux is unsupported because
  the pin and signature checks cover only Windows and macOS.
- The native `.exe` is spawned without a shell; an npm `claude.cmd` shim is never
  used.

```

# 0003 · Authenticate the specialist with the user's Claude plan

## Context

The specialist can authenticate with the user's Claude subscription
(`claude auth login --claudeai`), with an Anthropic API key, or through Bedrock,
Vertex or Foundry. The Agent SDK documentation states: "Unless previously approved,
Anthropic does not allow third party developers to offer claude.ai login or rate
limits for their products, including agents built on the Claude Agent SDK." This app
is a personal tool run by its author on their own machine with their own account.
Both reference projects already implement the subscription login flow: the app opens
only an Anthropic https URL, accepts the pasted code, and never reads the stored
credential.

## Decision

The specialist authenticates only with the user's own Claude plan login, inside the
app's isolated `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` are
stripped from the specialist's environment. Rejected: API-key authentication, by the
user's choice; and offering both, which adds a credential path nobody will use.

## Consequences

- The app is for personal use and must not be distributed to other users as is;
  distributing it requires a new ADR adding API-key or cloud-provider authentication.
- Specialist usage counts against the user's plan limits; `total_cost_usd` is shown
  as an estimate, not a charge.
- Rate-limit and auth failures surface as CLI text and are classified by pattern,
  which is brittle across CLI versions.

```

# 0004 · Sandbox delegated work in a read-only copy

## Context

Delegated analysis must reach only the files its task needs, start read-only, and
never change the user's originals without explicit approval. The host is Windows, so
there is no OS-level sandbox for a spawned process: Claude Code's permission rules
and DeepAgents' backends are policy enforced by the agent runtime, and a `Bash` tool
can step around both. The workspace already ships a dev container
(`.devcontainer/`) that can host command execution.

## Decision

Each task gets its own working directory under the app's data folder, into which the
app copies only the files the context package names. The orchestrator sees it through
a DeepAgents `FilesystemBackend` rooted there; the specialist gets it as `cwd` with
read-only tools (`Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`) and no `Bash`. Changes come back as a patch
against the copy, and the app applies it to the originals only after the user
approves it. Command execution is off by default and, when enabled, runs only inside
a container. Every file read or written is recorded in the task's audit log, and the
directory can be discarded when the task ends. Rejected: running the specialist in
the original repository with deny rules, because a rule is not a boundary; and a
container for every task, because most tasks only read.

## Consequences

- Files outside the copy-in list are unreachable, so a context package that omits a
  needed file produces a weaker answer rather than a wider read.
- Copying large trees costs time and disk; the copy-in list is the lever.
- Patches can conflict with originals that changed during the task; applying one
  checks the base first.
- Enabling commands requires Docker on the host.

```

---

# 0005 · Store events in SQLite with raw JSONL per task

## Context

Every agent action becomes an event: task, agent, time, state, inputs and outputs,
tools, files, errors, usage and cost. The UI shows them live and in history, and they
serve audit and diagnosis. `study-lab` keeps jobs in memory only, so a crash loses
them, and stores data in `node:sqlite` with `user_version` migrations. The MagnoTech
app keeps append-only JSONL per project but makes the UI re-read every file on each
change, which is O(n) per event, and does not keep the raw CLI stream.

## Decision

Tasks, steps and normalized events live in SQLite (`node:sqlite`, `user_version`
migrations, as in `study-lab`). Each task also appends the raw stream of every agent,
unparsed, to its own JSONL file. Secrets are redacted before either write. The UI
receives each new event as an incremental IPC message and queries SQLite for history.
On start, tasks left running are marked interrupted. Rejected: JSONL only, which
cannot answer history and cost queries without a full scan; and SQLite only, which
loses the raw evidence needed when the parser misreads an event.

## Consequences

- Two stores to keep consistent; the JSONL is the source when they disagree about a
  raw event, SQLite for everything derived.
- `node:sqlite` is still experimental and tied to the Node bundled with Electron.
- Redaction must run before the write; a secret that reaches disk stays in the
  audit trail.

```

`docs/adr/0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task.md`:

---
status: accepted
---

# 0006 · Run the specialist inside a container per task

## Context

adr:0004-sandbox-delegated-work-in-a-read-only-copy ran the specialist on the host
with the task directory as `cwd` and kept containers for command execution only. On
Windows that leaves the specialist's process with the user's account: tool
restrictions and `--setting-sources ""` are policy, not a boundary, and the host's
paths, username and environment are visible to anything it runs. The user asked for
each delegation to run inside a sandbox mounted as `workspace/<uuid>/:/work/`, seeing
only the objective of its own step. Claude Code publishes a reference dev container
with a default-deny egress firewall for this kind of isolation, and lists the
domains it needs in its network requirements. Docker Desktop is installed on the
host but was not running when this was decided.

## Decision

Every delegation runs the pinned Claude Code CLI in a fresh Linux container. The
host directory `<userData>/workspace/<uuid>/`, holding only the copied files, is mounted
at `/work`, read-only unless the step is in modify mode; the only other bind mount is
the run's rendered system prompt, read-only and outside `/work`.
Login state lives in a named volume shared by those containers, never in the user's
`~/.claude`. The container runs as a non-root user with every capability dropped,
`no-new-privileges`, a read-only root filesystem and resource limits, and reaches
the network only through an egress proxy that allows Claude Code's required domains.
The CLI is baked into an image built from a Dockerfile in this repository, pinned by
version and verified against the signed release manifest. If Docker is unavailable
the app refuses to delegate rather than falling back to the host. Rejected: the host
process of adr:0004-sandbox-delegated-work-in-a-read-only-copy, for the reasons
above; and the reference `init-firewall.sh` inside the agent container, because it
needs `NET_ADMIN` and `NET_RAW` in the very container being confined.

## Consequences

- Docker Desktop is a hard requirement for delegation.
- The specialist runs the Linux build of the CLI; the Windows binary verification in
  adr:0002-run-the-specialist-through-the-pinned-claude-code-cli no longer applies
  to it, and verification moves to the image build.
- Subscription login happens inside a container, and the login volume is readable
  by every specialist run.
- Container start adds seconds to each delegation.
- The copy-in workspace, patch approval, audit log and discard of
  adr:0004-sandbox-delegated-work-in-a-read-only-copy carry over unchanged.

```

`docs/adr/0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container.md`:

# 0007 · Run the orchestrator's tools in a task container

## Context

adr:0001-use-deepagents-on-openrouter-for-orchestration left the orchestrator's tools in
the Electron main process: DeepAgents read the source folder through a `FilesystemBackend`
on the host, and its `execute` tool had no backend that could run a command. The user asked
for every agent to run in a sandbox, with the orchestrator seeing the whole source folder
through a local bind and the specialist seeing only the workspace prepared for its step,
under adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task. The user also asked that
the orchestrator write the prompt handed to the specialist: a brief stating the background
and purpose of the step, in the orchestrator's words, instead of a prompt assembled only
from structured fields. DeepAgents provides `BaseSandbox`, a backend whose file tools and
`execute` all run through one `execute(command)` call, so a container can stand behind it.

## Decision

Each task starts one container, `hfr-orch-<task>`, from the specialist image, with the
source folder bind-mounted read-only at `/workspace`, no network, a non-root user, every
capability dropped, `no-new-privileges`, a read-only root and resource limits. The
orchestrator's `ls`, `read_file`, `glob`, `grep` and `execute` run in it through a
`BaseSandbox` over `docker exec`; uploads are refused, so nothing the orchestrator does
writes the user's files. The container is removed when the task ends. The agent loop and
its calls to OpenRouter stay in the main process. The context package gains a `brief`
written by the orchestrator; the sandbox replaces any host or `/workspace` path in it with
`/work`, and renders it first in the specialist's prompt. Rejected: running the whole
orchestrator in a container, which would move the event log, approvals and the app's IPC
across a container boundary for no gain in isolation of the user's files; and a writable
bind, which would let `execute` change the originals without patch approval.

## Consequences

- Docker is required to start a task, not only to delegate.
- `execute` becomes available to the orchestrator, confined to a networkless container;
  build or test commands that need to write fail on the read-only bind.
- The specialist's prompt now carries free text from the orchestrator, so R3.2 of
  `specs/task-sandbox/` holds by scrubbing rather than by construction; the user's request
  can reach the specialist as far as the orchestrator restates it.
- The brief must state the real purpose and ownership; the orchestrator's system prompt
  forbids inventing either.

```

# 0008 · Ask the user from the specialist over the run channel

## Context

The chat lets either agent ask the user a question mid-run (specs/chat R5). The
orchestrator runs in the Electron main process, so its `ask_user` tool just holds a
promise the UI resolves. The specialist does not: it runs the Claude Code CLI inside a
per-delegation container with every capability dropped and no network but the egress
proxy to Claude's own hosts (adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task).
For it to ask the user, an answer has to cross that boundary and come back, without
opening a second way out of a container built to have none. The run's rendered system
prompt is already bind-mounted into the container, read-only, outside `/work`, so a
host⇄container channel in that same run directory needs no new network and no new
privilege — only a writable file beside an existing mount. The reference project's PoC
used exactly this, a file-based channel polled on both sides.

## Decision

The specialist asks the user through a small MCP server baked into the specialist
image and registered on the CLI's `claudeArgs`. Its one tool writes the question as a
file in the run directory — mounted writable for this purpose, still outside `/work`
and separate from the read-only source — and blocks polling for an answer file. The
host watches the run directory, surfaces the question in the chat, writes the user's
answer (or the default on timeout) to the answer file, and the tool returns it with
its origin. No network path is opened: the channel is the shared directory, nothing
else. Rejected: a local socket or an HTTP endpoint, which is a second listener to
confine inside a container whose whole point is to have no network; and widening the
egress allowlist, which would route a question through Claude's hosts and conflate it
with the specialist's own traffic.

## Consequences

- The specialist image now carries the MCP server; it moves with the pinned CLI
  version (adr:0002-run-the-specialist-through-the-pinned-claude-code-cli), and the
  `claudeArgs` and the run-directory mount in `src/main/sandbox/docker.ts` change as a
  tested change to the sandbox boundary.
- The run directory becomes a two-way channel, not only an input; its contents are
  redacted and bounded like any other agent output before reaching the UI.
- A delegation can block on the user. The approval and question timeouts (specs/chat
  R4.5, R5.4) bound that wait; the task's cancel still aborts the container.
- The specialist can ask for input that steers its analysis, so the same prohibition
  the orchestrator's brief carries — no invented authorization or purpose — is stated
  to the specialist too.

```

`docs/adr/0009-give-the-orchestrator-a-writable-scratch.md`:

# 0009 · Give the orchestrator a writable scratch

## Context

The harness divides the work: the specialist reasons about the target's code, and the
orchestrator dispatches, organises files and writes code that builds on the
specialist's findings — scripts it runs to test a hypothesis, probes, small tools
(specs/chat R6). adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container gave the
orchestrator a container with the source bind-mounted read-only and a read-only root,
so `execute` can read and run against the source but can write nowhere. That is what
keeps the user's files unchanged without patch approval, and it must stay. But code
the orchestrator writes to test a hypothesis has nowhere to live or run, and the
read-only source mount is deliberately not that place.

## Decision

The orchestrator's container gains one writable mount, `/scratch`, a per-task
directory under the app's data folder (or a tmpfs where the experiment needs no
persistence), separate from the read-only source bind and from `/work`. `execute`
writes and runs there; the source mount stays read-only and uploads stay refused, so
nothing the orchestrator runs can change the user's files. The scratch is removed with
the task's container. A change to the user's source remains a specialist patch through
the existing approval (specs/chat R6.4). Rejected: making the source mount writable,
which would let `execute` change the originals with no approval and defeat
adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container; and writing experiments into
`/work`, which is the specialist's prepared workspace, not the orchestrator's.

## Consequences

- `src/main/sandbox/docker.ts` adds the `/scratch` mount for the orchestrator
  container; this is a change to the sandbox boundary and is tested as one.
- The orchestrator can run code with real side effects within the container — files,
  processes — but still no network (the container keeps adr:0007's no-network rule),
  so an experiment cannot reach out.
- Scratch contents are the orchestrator's working state, not evidence; what it carries
  into its answer is still tied to files and lines like any other claim.
- The scratch is per task and discarded with it; nothing an experiment writes
  survives, which a later task must not depend on.

```

# 0010 · Build the renderer on shadcn/ui and Radix

## Context

The renderer began with a handful of primitives written in the shadcn/ui style — a button,
a badge, a card, inputs — and no Radix, because no view needed more than that. The chat
(specs/chat R7) changes the surface: a conversation that scrolls on its own while the
composer stays put, collapsible tool calls, an approval card with an argument editor, a
question card per kind with radio choices and toggles, tooltips on turn controls, and a
side panel of tabs. Each of those is a component with keyboard and focus behaviour and
ARIA roles that are easy to get subtly wrong by hand. The user asked for the app to be
built with shadcn/ui. shadcn/ui is not a dependency: its components are source copied into
the project, built on Radix primitives, `class-variance-authority`, `clsx` and
`tailwind-merge` — the last three already adopted — and themed through CSS variables that
Tailwind v4 maps with `@theme inline`.

## Decision

The renderer's components are shadcn/ui components, kept as source under
`src/renderer/src/components/ui/`, one file each, on the unified `radix-ui` package, pinned.
The theme moves to shadcn/ui's token names (`background`, `card`, `muted-foreground`,
`primary`, `border`, `ring`, `destructive`, …) set to the app's existing dark palette, plus
`success` and `warning` for task states; the app's own names (`panel`, `raised`, `line`,
`ink`) go. Components are added by copying their source, adjusted to the app's density,
not through the shadcn CLI, which assumes a single-root Vite or Next project layout that
electron-vite does not have. Rejected: keeping hand-written primitives, which would mean
writing a scroll area, radio group, tabs and tooltip with their accessibility by hand; and
a styled component library, which ships its own theme and runtime instead of source the
project owns.

## Consequences

- `radix-ui` is a new dependency in `docs/stack.md`; a component that needs another package
  (an animation helper, a date picker) is a new decision, not something pulled in with a copy.
- Every view uses the shadcn/ui token names; a raw color in a view is a finding in review.
- Component source is the project's to change, so an upstream shadcn/ui fix is copied in by
  hand, not upgraded; the copies say what they are and stay close to upstream.
- Radix renders some inline styles; the renderer's CSP already allows inline styles and
  keeps scripts to the app itself.

```

`docs/adr/0011-limit-the-orchestrator-to-planning-delegation-and-its-own-code.md`:

```md
---
status: accepted
---

# 0011 · Limit the orchestrator to planning, delegation and its own code

## Context

The harness splits the work by cost and skill. The orchestrator is a coding assistant
on a cheap OpenRouter model — the user means Chinese coding models such as DeepSeek —
that plans the task, prepares each analysis and writes the code. The specialist, Claude
Opus in its own container, does the deep research and the reverse engineering. The flow
the user wants: the orchestrator needs part of a binary understood, prepares a sandbox
holding only the context and files that analysis needs, delegates it, and writes code
from what the specialist returns. adr:0009-give-the-orchestrator-a-writable-scratch gave
the orchestrator `/scratch` and `execute` for that code, and specs/chat R6.1 asked it, in
its instructions only, to leave analysis to the specialist. A real task showed
instructions alone are weak: asked to analyse an APK, the orchestrator made 157 tool
calls of its own — a ZIP reader, an AXML decoder and a DEX parser in Perl — delegated
nothing, and answered from its own reading. DeepAgents binds a general-purpose `task`
subagent and `delete` besides the file tools, so the orchestrator could also hand the
analysis to a second cheap agent. And the orchestrator had no way to hand its own code
to the user, or to the specialist: only a specialist's modify-mode delegation produced
a patch, and a delegation carried only source files.

## Decision

The orchestrator keeps the tools a coding assistant needs: `write_todos`, `ls`, `glob`,
`read_file` and `grep` (to read the user's code it writes or integrates with),
`write_file`, `edit_file` and `execute` (whose writes land only in `/scratch`),
`delegate_to_specialist`, `propose_patch`, `apply_patch` and `ask_user`. A middleware in
`src/main/orchestrator/agent.ts` hides every other tool from the model and refuses a call
to one; it is an allowlist, so a tool a later DeepAgents release adds stays hidden. Its
instructions name it a coding assistant and send every analysis of the target —
disassembly, decompilation, formats, protocols, behaviour — to the specialist, with a
package complete enough for the analysis to run without obstacles and a report the
orchestrator can write code from (contracts, constants, test vectors). `propose_patch`
turns files the orchestrator wrote in `/scratch` into a patch against the current
originals, which `apply_patch` takes through the existing approval. A delegation may
carry files from `/scratch` — a harness, a script, code for the specialist to check
against the target — given to the specialist under `.orchestrator/` and never part of
a patch. adr:0009-give-the-orchestrator-a-writable-scratch and
adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container stand. Rejected: keeping
every tool, which leaves the `task` subagent as a second analyst; confining
`read_file` and `grep` to `/scratch`, which stops the orchestrator reading the code it
must integrate with; removing `execute` and having the specialist compile and test the
orchestrator's code, which costs an Opus run per test cycle; and a second container
with no source mounted for `execute`, which costs a container per task and splits the
file tools from `execute`.

## Consequences

- The orchestrator can still read the target with `read_file`, `grep` and `execute`;
  only its instructions keep it from analysing. If cheap models keep analysing anyway,
  confining what its container mounts is the next step.
- Every analysis costs a delegation, so a task spends more on the specialist; the
  orchestrator re-delegates when a report or its own tests do not hold.
- The orchestrator's patch is checked against the originals' hashes at proposal time
  like a specialist's, so a file changed in between is a conflict, not an overwrite.
- Files the orchestrator prepares reach the specialist's workspace but neither its
  snapshot nor a patch; a specialist edit to them is dropped.
- The allowlist hides tools from one model; it does not remove them from the graph,
  so the read-only container remains what keeps the source unchanged.

```

# 0012 · Pull the specialist's base image from GHCR

## Context

adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task builds the specialist image on
the user's machine from a Dockerfile in this repository, and the app treats the image
as ready when its tag and its `hfr.claude-code` label match the pinned Claude Code
version. The image's contents changed in specs/chat (the ask-user MCP server) while the
version stayed the same, and an image built before that change passed the check and
failed at the first question. The user asked for the app to check Docker and pull the
image at start instead of building it. The image holds the Claude Code binary, whose
licence grants no right to redistribute it, and this repository is public.

## Decision

Everything in the specialist's image except Claude Code — the Node base, the tools,
the non-root `agent` user, the ask-user MCP server — is a base image built by this
repository's CI and published to `ghcr.io/protonspy/hfr-specialist-base`, tagged by
the hash of its build context. The repository pins it by registry digest beside that
hash, and the test suite fails when the build context and the pin disagree. On the
user's machine the app pulls the pinned base and builds a short local layer that adds
only the Claude Code CLI, verified against its signed release manifest as
adr:0002-run-the-specialist-through-the-pinned-claude-code-cli requires, and labels
it with the Claude Code version and the base's digest reference. An image is ready
only when both labels match the app's pins. The app prepares a missing or stale
image at start, without being asked. Rejected: publishing the whole image with the
CLI, publicly (redistributes the binary) or privately (needs a registry login on
every machine); and keeping the full local build with a recipe hash label, which
leaves every install to build the whole image.

## Consequences

- A change to the base's build context is published by CI and then re-pinned in the
  repository; a pin the context has moved past fails the tests rather than shipping.
- The package on GHCR must be public for an anonymous pull.
- Preparing the image needs the network on the user's machine: to GHCR for the base,
  and to Anthropic's release host for the CLI.
- The image is linux/amd64 only.

```

# 0013 · Give the sandboxes full internet access

## Context

adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task routes the specialist's
traffic through an egress proxy, `hfr-egress`, on an internal network, allowing only
the domains Claude Code requires, and
adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container runs the orchestrator's task
container with no network. The user decided that a sandbox is a controlled
environment scoped to the analysis — the files the agent can reach — and not a
network jail: the specialist has to download and install the tools an analysis needs,
the orchestrator's own code has to fetch its dependencies, and internet access is
essential to both.

## Decision

Both sandboxes run on Docker's default bridge network with full internet access. The
egress proxy, its image, its allowlist and the internal `hfr-sandbox` network are
removed, and the app removes a proxy container and network an earlier version left
behind. Everything else adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task and
adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container confine stays: the copied
files as the only bind mounts, the read-only source, the non-root user, dropped
capabilities, resource limits, and no host path or environment. This supersedes the
egress proxy part of adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task and the
no-network part of adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container. Rejected:
widening the allowlist per tool, which the user ruled out as an obstacle to the
analysis.

## Consequences

- Isolation rests on what is mounted. Content inside an analysed artifact that steers
  the agent (prompt injection) can send out the files in `/work` or `/scratch` and the
  specialist's Claude login token on the shared config volume; nothing on the network
  stops it.
- Nothing beyond the files a task needs may ever be mounted into either sandbox.
- A delegation no longer depends on a proxy container being up.
- The ask channel of adr:0008-ask-the-user-from-the-specialist-over-the-run-channel is
  no longer the specialist's only way out; it stays the only way to the user.

`docs/adr/0014-add-openai-compatible-orchestrator-providers.md`:

# 0014 · Add OpenAI-compatible orchestrator providers

## Context

adr:0001-use-deepagents-on-openrouter-for-orchestration ties the orchestrator to
OpenRouter: one key, one client, OpenRouter's routing fields on every request. The
user wants to run it on a provider key of their own, DeepSeek first, without an
OpenRouter account. DeepSeek, like most hosted and local model servers, implements the
OpenAI chat completions API, so it needs a base URL, an API key and a model name and
nothing more.

## Decision

The orchestrator's model is chosen by a provider setting: `openrouter` (unchanged),
`deepseek`, or `custom`. The last two use `ChatOpenAI` from `@langchain/openai` at the
provider's base URL; DeepSeek is a preset (`https://api.deepseek.com`, `deepseek-chat`)
and `custom` is any other endpoint. A provider is one entry in `src/shared/providers.ts`.
Each provider keeps its own key, encrypted as before; OpenRouter's keeps its original
storage slot so an existing install is unaffected. Reasoning effort is sent as
`reasoning_effort` on these providers. The specialist (adr:0002-run-the-specialist-through-the-pinned-claude-code-cli)
and the sandbox are untouched. Rejected: a dedicated `@langchain/deepseek` client,
which would add a dependency and one more code path for what a base URL already covers.

## Consequences

- OpenRouter's `models` fallback and `provider.data_collection: deny` have no
  equivalent on the other providers: source code goes to that provider under its own
  terms, and the user chooses it knowingly.
- These APIs report tokens but no cost, so the orchestrator's cost for a task is 0
  on them; the specialist's cost is unchanged.
- Models that return a separate reasoning channel and require it to be sent back across
  tool calls (such as `deepseek-reasoner`) are not supported through the plain OpenAI
  client; the DeepSeek preset is `deepseek-chat`.
- A custom base URL may be plain `http` (a local server) but never carries credentials in it.

`docs/adr/0015-run-the-task-container-as-root.md`:

```md
---
status: accepted

# 0015 · Run the task container as root

## Context

adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container runs the orchestrator's task
container as the non-root `agent` user, with every capability dropped and a read-only
root filesystem; adr:0009-give-the-orchestrator-a-writable-scratch adds `/scratch` as
its one writable place. In a real run the orchestrator's code needed `unzip` and
`python3`, and `apt-get install` failed with "are you root?". The user decided that a
sandbox is a controlled environment scoped to the analysis, free to install any tool
(adr:0013-give-the-sandboxes-full-internet-access); what keeps the user's files safe
is the read-only bind of the source, not the container's user.

## Decision

The task container runs as root, with a writable root filesystem and only the
capabilities installing packages needs — `CHOWN`, `DAC_OVERRIDE`, `FOWNER`, `FSETID`,
`SETUID`, `SETGID`, `KILL` — so the orchestrator can install packages with `apt-get`
and anything else its code needs; `NET_RAW`, `MKNOD` and the rest stay dropped. It keeps `no-new-privileges`, its resource limits, and the source
folder bind-mounted read-only and recursively so; it is never `--privileged` and never
gets the Docker socket or any other host path. The container and everything installed
in it are removed with the task. Rejected: installing into the user's space only,
which leaves out every tool that comes as a system package; and baking a fixed tool set
into the base image, which cannot guess what an analysis will need.

## Consequences

- Root in the container cannot write the source: the bind is read-only for root too.
- A container escape now starts from root inside the container, with those seven
  capabilities, rather than from an unprivileged user.
- The writable layer has no size cap: a runaway install can fill Docker's disk until
  the task ends.
- What the orchestrator installs lasts for the task only; a later task starts clean.
- The specialist's container is unchanged here; it gains the same freedom with its
  shell under specs/rea-native.

`docs/adr/0016-let-the-orchestrator-run-the-specialists-sandbox.md`:

---
status: accepted

# 0016 · Let the orchestrator run the specialist's sandbox

## Context

adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task gives every delegation a fresh
container that lives exactly as long as the Claude Code process: a non-root user, every
capability dropped, a read-only root filesystem, and only `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` (plus
`Edit` and `Write` in modify mode). In a real task the orchestrator concluded "the
specialist sandbox has no shell — only file reading", so it unpacked and dumped the target
itself and handed the specialist text to interpret, which is the analysis
adr:0011-limit-the-orchestrator-to-planning-delegation-and-its-own-code sends to the
specialist. The user decided that the sandbox must run as `root:root`, that the
orchestrator sets its CPU, memory and disk, copies files from the task's source folder into
its workspace, runs any command in it and installs dependencies, and that the specialist
works in the sandbox the orchestrator prepared. adr:0015-run-the-task-container-as-root
already gave the orchestrator's own container the same freedom. Docker Desktop on this host
uses the containerd snapshotter, which accepts `--storage-opt size=` and ignores it (a
container capped at 1 GB wrote 1.5 GB), while `docker container inspect --size` reports the
writable layer's size.

## Decision

The orchestrator creates a sandbox with no limit unless it sets one: CPUs, memory, disk and
processes are each optional, and none comes from the app. A sandbox is a long-lived
container, `hfr-sbx-<id>`, from the specialist image: root, a writable root filesystem,
`no-new-privileges`, every capability dropped but those installing packages needs (the set
of adr:0015-run-the-task-container-as-root), Docker's default network, the shared login
volume, and three binds: `workspace/<id>/` writable at `/work`, `runs/<id>/` read-only at
`/run/hfr`, and its ask channel. It is never `--privileged`, never gets the Docker socket
and never another host path. The orchestrator copies files into `/work` only from the
task's source folder and from its own scratch, runs commands in the sandbox as root, and
delegates into it, one delegation at a time; the sandbox outlives each delegation and is
removed when the orchestrator destroys it or the task ends. The specialist runs as root
with `Bash` besides its file tools, still `--restricted` with no setting source and every
permission prompt denied; a delegation that names no sandbox gets a container of its own
with the same user, capabilities and tools, and, as the user ruled the sandboxes too
limited, no memory, CPU, process or size limit and no cap on the files copied into it;
the limits leave Settings. A disk limit the orchestrator sets is enforced by watching: the
app adds the writable layer's size to the workspace's and stops the sandbox once the total
passes its limit. After every specialist run the login volume is handed back to the
non-root user the login container runs as. The orchestrator's own task container
(adr:0015-run-the-task-container-as-root) loses every limit: no memory, CPU or process
limit, and its `/scratch` and `/tmp` move from size-capped tmpfs mounts to folders on its
writable root, on Docker's disk rather than in memory, since the user ruled that the
orchestrator's sandbox has no limit. Rejected: a `--storage-opt` quota, ignored on
this Docker; a tmpfs `/work`, which spends the host's memory as disk and leaves the rest of
the filesystem unbounded; a ceiling in Settings, which the user declined; copying from any
host path, which a container with full internet access
(adr:0013-give-the-sandboxes-full-internet-access) could send anywhere.

## Consequences

- The login volume, with the subscription token, is mounted in every sandbox from its start.
  The specialist can read it with its shell, and so can the orchestrator's model through
  `sandbox_exec`, whose output goes to OpenRouter; the redaction of known secret shapes masks
  a plain read, not a deliberate one, and full internet access already lets either send it
  anywhere. The exposure is accepted for now; handing the token to a sandbox only for the
  length of a delegation is the change that would narrow it.
- A disk limit is enforced after the fact: a sandbox can pass its limit by what it writes between
  two checks before it is stopped.
- The orchestrator can analyse the target with `sandbox_exec` as it could with `execute`;
  only its instructions send that work to the specialist.
- In modify mode every file left in `/work` that was not copied in becomes an added file of
  the patch, so both agents are told to keep their own output outside `/work`.
- A container escape starts from root with seven capabilities in the specialist's
  container too.
- Every container the app starts, but the login container, can take all of Docker's
  memory, CPUs and disk unless the orchestrator limited its sandbox; a runaway process is
  stopped by Docker Desktop's own VM limits, by `sandbox_destroy` or by ending the task.
- A large target goes from the source folder to the workspace whole, on the app's data
  disk, as many times as it is delegated without a sandbox.

```

# 0017 · Keep a task's conversation, containers and files until it is deleted

## Context

A task's conversation lives in LangGraph's `MemorySaver`, so it is gone when the app quits;
`recover()` then closes every conversation and a task can only be retried from its request.
Cancelling or closing a task removes its task container (adr:0015-run-the-task-container-as-root)
and its sandboxes (adr:0016-let-the-orchestrator-run-the-specialists-sandbox), and with them
`/scratch`, every tool installed and everything the specialist extracted; discard on completion
deletes each delegation's workspace as it ends. The user ruled that nothing may be lost when a
container goes: a cancelled task, reopened, continues from where it stopped, with its history and
the files already analysed. The stack keeps no native module (`node:sqlite`,
adr:0005-store-events-in-sqlite-with-raw-jsonl-per-task), and LangGraph's SQLite saver is built
on `better-sqlite3`.

## Decision

A task keeps its conversation, containers and files until the user deletes it. The checkpointer
is `MemorySaver` with every checkpoint and write also stored in the app's SQLite database and a
thread loaded back from it when the task reopens, so LangGraph's own logic keeps deciding what a
checkpoint holds. Every file of a task lives under `<userData>/tasks/<taskId>/`: the
orchestrator's `/scratch`, now a writable bind of `tasks/<id>/scratch` rather than a folder in
the container, each delegation's workspace, run directory and snapshot, and each sandbox's
`/work` and the specialist's own `/root/out`, also bound from there. Containers lose `--rm`:
cancelling, closing or quitting stops them, reopening starts them, and one Docker no longer has
is created again over the same folders, with the orchestrator told that installed tools were
reset. Sandboxes are recorded in the database so a reopened task reaches them by the same id.
Cancelled, failed, interrupted and closed tasks reopen on the user's message or on Continue.
Deleting the task — refused while it runs — removes its containers, folder, patches,
conversation and records; nothing else does, and the discard setting goes. Rejected:
LangGraph's SQLite saver, a native module the stack avoids; `docker commit` of each container on
stop, which keeps installed tools but costs gigabytes per task; keeping files only in the
containers, which a `docker system prune` or a Docker reset erases.

## Consequences

- Disk grows with every task until the user deletes it; the app does not clean up by itself.
- Two more host folders are mounted per container: `/scratch` in the task container and
  `/root/out` in a sandbox, each the task's own folder; nothing outside `tasks/<id>/` is mounted.
- Stopped containers stay in Docker and appear in `docker ps -a`; starting the app no longer
  removes them.
- What a tool installed survives a stop but not a container Docker removed; the files do.
- A delegation cut off mid-run is not resumed inside Claude Code: the orchestrator delegates
  again, over the files that remain.
- What containers write — samples, extracted payloads, links, special files — stays on the host
  under `%AppData%` until the task is deleted; the app never opens or runs anything there, and
  deleting removes each entry with `unlink`, never following a link.
- A container is reused only while it carries the fingerprint of the arguments the app would
  create it with now; one made by an older app, with another image or boundary, is created
  again over the same folders.

```

# 0018 · Make REA native to the specialist

## Context

The specialist does the reverse engineering, and the user wants it to work as a harness of REA
(see the wiki page rea-in-the-sandbox): REA's MCP server attached, its skill, and an operating guide in the role
of an `AGENTS.md`, so that every analysis follows REA's workflow and evidence model.

Today the specialist starts with `--setting-sources ""` and `--strict-mcp-config`, so nothing from
a settings file, a skills folder or an `AGENTS.md` loads. Its only MCP server is the ask-user one
(adr:0008-ask-the-user-from-the-specialist-over-the-run-channel).

REA installs no engines. Native decompilation needs Ghidra and a JDK 21, which Debian bookworm
does not ship, and Android needs JADX and Apktool. The user chose to bake REA, Ghidra and the
Android tools into the image, and to give REA to the specialist only. Reports cite evidence as
`path:lines`, which drops REA's `ev_…` and `unk_…` identifiers and every address in a binary.

## Decision

**The image.** The published base image (adr:0012-pull-the-specialists-base-image-from-ghcr)
carries, each pinned by version and checked against its SHA-256 at build:

- `rea-agents` 6.8.0, with every dependency from a lockfile committed beside the Dockerfile,
  installed with `npm ci` without optional packages or install scripts;
- Ghidra 12.1.4;
- Temurin JDK 21;
- jadx-headless-mcp 0.7.1;
- Apktool 3.0.3.

The image also holds REA's whole skill directory at `/opt/hfr/rea-skill/`, and the specialist's
operating guide, `sandbox/specialist-base/AGENTS.md`, at `/opt/hfr/AGENTS.md`. The engines' paths
are set as image environment variables.

**The specialist.**

- Its MCP configuration adds REA as a stdio server (`rea.mjs mcp`) beside ask-user, and its
  allowed tools add `mcp__rea`.
- Its environment gains an MCP tool timeout long enough for Ghidra's cold start.
- Its system prompt renders the operating guide from the same file the image carries, and
  points to the skill to read first.
- `rea setup` is never run.

**Output.** A delegation's own container binds an output folder of the task's at `/root/out`, as
a sandbox does (adr:0017-keep-a-tasks-conversation-containers-and-files-until-it-is-deleted).
The specialist exports its evidence bundle there.

**Evidence citations.** A report's evidence lines may cite an REA evidence or unknown id, or an
address in a file, besides a line range.

**The orchestrator.** It is given no REA tool and no REA instructions. Its task container runs
the same image, so the binaries are present there, unused.

**Rejected:**

- Loading the skill through `rea setup` or a skills folder, which `--setting-sources ""`
  ignores. Lifting that flag would let a sample's planted settings load.
- Installing engines per sandbox at run time, which costs minutes for each new sandbox.
- A separate image for the orchestrator, which costs a second published image while its
  instructions already keep it from analysing.

## Consequences

- The base image grows by about 1.2 GB, and its CI build takes longer. A version bump of any
  engine is a re-pinned, tested change, like the Claude Code pin.
- REA's 229-tool catalog is in every specialist session. Claude Code's tool search keeps it out
  of the context on the user's plan; an endpoint that disables tool search would pay for it.
- The specialist can still run tools it installs itself (adr:0016-let-the-orchestrator-run-the-specialists-sandbox);
  REA is the default path, not the only one.
- REA's evidence ledger lives in its server process: what the specialist does not export to
  `/root/out` is gone when the run ends.
- The orchestrator could run `rea` through `execute`; only its instructions stop it. A separate
  image is the next step if it does.
- REA's tools take any path inside the container, so the rule that keeps Claude Code's file tools
  out of the login volume does not bind them; with root `Bash` already able to read it, this
  widens nothing. Several REA tools run code (process capture, Rizin commands), as `Bash` does.
- An REA id in a report is cited, not checked: nothing compares it with the exported bundle.

```

# 0019 · Keep the specialist's brief technical

## Context

adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container gave the context package a `brief` written
by the orchestrator, and specs/orchestrator R2.7 asked it to state the background and real purpose
of each step: what the system is, who owns it, why the analysis is done. In practice the
orchestrator relays the user's request into it ("the user asked for this, in order to do that").

The user ruled the opposite. The specialist does a deep technical analysis and needs only its
technical scope: the artifact, what is known about it, and what to find. It is isolated by the
files the orchestrator mounts, and its prompt should be limited to the scope of that discovery.
The app's own statement that the artifacts in `/work` are owned by the user or authorized for
analysis (specs/task-sandbox R3.4) is not part of the brief and stays.

## Decision

The brief is technical only. It states:

- what the artifact is: its format, platform, architecture, language, toolchain and versions;
- what is already established about it, with the evidence an earlier delegation returned;
- what the step must map or discover.

It never mentions the user, their request, who they are, what they intend, or why the work is
being done, and it never invents ownership, authorization or purpose. The whole context package
is written in English, whatever language the user writes in, while the orchestrator answers the
user in theirs. The objective is phrased
the same way: "I have file X and need to map Y". The orchestrator's instructions, the package
schema's description of `brief`, and the glossary say so.

Rejected:

- Dropping the `brief` field, which still carries the technical background the objective alone
  does not.
- Filtering briefs in the app for words like "user", which would also catch technical terms
  such as "user-agent" and "user mode".

## Consequences

- The specialist no longer reads the user's goal, so it cannot weigh one technical path against
  another by what the user wants. The orchestrator has to turn that goal into explicit questions,
  constraints and a report format.
- The rule is held by the orchestrator's instructions alone; nothing in the app rejects a brief
  that relays the user's request.
- R2.7 of specs/orchestrator and the brief consequence of
  adr:0007-run-the-orchestrators-tools-in-a-task-container are replaced by this record.

```

# 0020 · Group tasks into projects that share their analyses

## Context

A task names a source folder and stands alone. Its conversation, containers, sandboxes and files are
its own (adr:0017-keep-a-tasks-conversation-containers-and-files-until-it-is-deleted), so a second
task on the same APK starts from nothing: it re-extracts, re-installs and re-delegates what the first
one already established.

The user asked for projects in the spirit of rebuild tools such as craft-anything (see the wiki).
A project is one target set up through guided choices, with its own UUID and workspace, and every
analysis is kept. The choices are the goal, the target with its detected kind, and the model and
effort. The user also asked that the tasks of a project share its sandboxes, outputs and analyses,
and that the project's folder default to the app's data folder with the option of another.

## Decision

A project owns one target and any number of tasks.

**Its own:**

- a UUID;
- a folder, `<userData>/projects/<uuid>/` or under a folder the user chose;
- a goal;
- the provider, model and efforts its tasks run with.

**The target.** A file target is copied into the project's `target/` folder, and that folder is what
tasks mount read-only. A folder target is mounted in place, read-only, as before. Copying keeps a
file's siblings, a Downloads folder say, out of every container.

**Shared by its tasks:**

- *Sandboxes.* The project's sandboxes, which become project-scoped records, so any of its tasks
  reaches one by id. One object per project in the main process holds the one-delegation-at-a-time
  rule across tasks.
- *Outputs.* Each task's folder lives under the project's folder.
- *Analyses.* The orchestrator reads the project's earlier delegation steps — objective, report,
  evidence — through two read-only tools, and is told how many exist when a task starts.

**Upgrade.** Tasks from before projects are moved into one project per source folder, with the app's
data folder as the project's folder, so their files stay where they are.

**Rejected:**

- Copying earlier reports into every new task's prompt, which grows each prompt with analyses the
  task may not need.
- Sharing the orchestrator's conversation between tasks, which would merge unrelated threads.
- Mounting a file target's parent folder, which exposes its siblings.

## Consequences

- Two tasks of a project can run at once, and they queue on a shared sandbox rather than run in it
  together.
- Deleting a project deletes its tasks. A folder the user chose is kept, and only what the app
  created inside it goes.
- A target file is stored twice on disk: the user's original and the project's copy.
- What one task's specialist writes to a shared sandbox's `/work` is visible to the next task's
  delegations there. That is the point, and also how a mistake carries over.
- An analysis is stored and replayed to every later task of the project, so text a hostile target
  planted in a report outlives its task. The orchestrator reads analyses as evidence marked as
  coming from the target, never as instructions, and reads each up to a size cap.

```

`docs/adr/0021-answer-the-specialist-from-the-orchestrator-and-let-the-user-decide-a-refusal.md`:
