# 0021 · Answer the specialist from the orchestrator, and let the user decide a refusal

## Context

adr:0008-ask-the-user-from-the-specialist-over-the-run-channel sends every question the specialist
asks to the user. In use, most of those questions are about the step itself — which file to start
from, whether a format is the one the brief named, what an earlier delegation found — and the
orchestrator, which wrote the context package, could answer them. Each one still stopped the
delegation until the user came back, or until the question timed out into its default.

plans/specialist-rea.md also planned a safeguard refusal — the specialist declining a step under
its usage policy — as a failure answered by one re-delegation carrying the purpose and
authorization the user states. That collides with adr:0019-keep-the-specialists-brief-technical:
the brief never carries the user's purpose, and a re-delegation reworded until it passes is the
one thing the user ruled out. Meanwhile a refusal came back to the orchestrator as an ordinary
`ERROR:` string, indistinguishable from a crash, and it retried or worked around it on its own.

## Decision

A question from the specialist goes first to one call of the orchestrator's model, with the
delegation's context package and the question, outside the task's conversation. The model either
answers it, and the answer returns over the run channel with its origin recorded as the
orchestrator, or says the question needs a fact only the user has, and only then is it put to the
user as adr:0008 describes. The channel, its files and its bounds are unchanged.

A safeguard refusal is its own state: its own event kind and step state, distinct from the app's
`sandbox.refused`, and the delegation tool tells the orchestrator it was a refusal. The task then
waits on the user, who chooses to stop the task, skip the step, or ask for a different technical
approach in their own words; that choice is what the orchestrator receives. The choice has no
timeout and is not counted against the question cap. Nothing in the app rewords the request or
adds a purpose or authorization to the brief.

Rejected:

- Every question to the user, as before: the cost this record exists to remove.
- Letting the orchestrator answer inside its own conversation: the delegation is one tool call
  mid-turn, and a nested turn on the same thread would interleave with it.
- One automatic re-delegation of a refused step with the user's stated purpose: it contradicts
  adr:0019 and turns a refusal into a rewording loop.

## Consequences

- The user-first part of adr:0008 and the re-delegation sentence of plans/specialist-rea.md are
  replaced by this record; specs/chat R5.2, R5.4 and R5.5 carry the change.
- A question costs one extra model call on the orchestrator's provider, spent even when the
  answer ends up being the user's.
- The orchestrator's model can answer wrongly where the user would have known better. It sees only
  the package it wrote, and it is told to pass anything outside that package to the user.
- A refused task can wait indefinitely; the user's stop or the task's cancel still ends it.

```

# 0022 · Run the TUI on Bun with OpenTUI

## Context

plans/finish-the-harness asks for a terminal UI beside the Electron app, on the same core: the event
log on `node:sqlite`, the orchestrator on DeepAgents and LangGraph, the delegations to the
specialist in Docker. The renderer the plan names, OpenTUI, runs on Bun: its core is a native
library loaded through `bun:ffi`. Whether the core runs on Bun was the open question — `node:sqlite`
is a Node built-in, and the main process relies on electron-vite for the `@shared/*` alias and for
Vite's `?raw` imports.

The spike (plan task 1.7, `tests/bun-core.test.ts`) ran one task with a delegation end to end under
Bun 1.4.4 on Windows: `node:sqlite`, the event log, DeepAgents and LangGraph against a scripted
OpenRouter, and the fake specialist, reaching `awaiting-user` with every event the Node suite sees.
Bun resolved the alias from the root `tsconfig.json` and the `?raw` import on its own. OpenTUI
0.8.1 rendered under Bun on Windows. The only Electron-only modules in `src/main` are `index.ts` and
`credentials.ts` (`safeStorage`).

## Decision

The TUI runs on Bun and renders with OpenTUI (`@opentui/core`), importing the core from `src/main`
and `src/shared` as it is, with Electron's parts — the key store and the transport between core and
view — behind interfaces the desktop app and the TUI each implement (plan task 1.8). The root
`tsconfig.json` carries the `@shared/*` path so Bun resolves it.

Rejected:

- Node with a Node terminal renderer (Ink, blessed): the core would run unchanged, but the plan
  names OpenTUI, and the spike removed the reason to give it up.
- A second core written for the terminal: two copies of the orchestrator and the event log would
  drift.

## Consequences

- Bun becomes a runtime of the project, beside Node and Electron's Node: a change to the core has
  to keep working under both, and `tests/bun-core.test.ts` (`HFR_BUN=1`) is the check.
- The TUI reaches users through Bun: the npm package and the release binaries carry or fetch it
  (specs/release).
- OpenTUI is young (0.x) and loads a native library per platform; an upgrade is a tested change.
- The key store needs an implementation outside Electron: the OS keychain, through the TUI's own
  dependency, where the desktop app keeps `safeStorage`.

```

# 0023 · Build the TUI on OpenTUI's React layer

## Context

adr:0022-run-the-tui-on-bun-with-opentui put the terminal UI on Bun and OpenTUI's core, and the 0.1
TUI drove `@opentui/core`'s renderables imperatively: one class per screen that adds, removes and
rewrites nodes by hand. plans/tui-revamp asks for a TUI at parity with the desktop app — a status
line, a transcript of markdown, collapsible tool calls and delegations, diffs, dialogs, a command
palette, a sidebar and every setup and settings screen — and every one of those is state drawn
into a tree that changes as pushes arrive. [[tui-0-1-defects]] lists what the imperative version
got wrong at a fraction of that size: lists that lose their place on every push, a whole timeline
redrawn as one text block, errors replaced by the next redraw.

OpenTUI ships two declarative layers over the same core: `@opentui/react`, a React reconciler,
and `@opentui/solid`, the one OpenCode's TUI is written on. Both render the same renderables —
`box`, `text`, `scrollbox`, `textarea`, `select`, `code`, `markdown`, `diff` — and both come with
a test renderer that draws a frame into a string and takes simulated keys.

The desktop app's renderer is React, and its view logic is already pure and framework-free in
`src/renderer/src/lib/`: the timeline that folds events into chat items (`timeline.ts`,
`chat.ts`), the history store that folds pushes (`store.ts`), the virtual window over a long list
(`virtual.ts`) and the formatting of tokens, costs and durations (`format.ts`).

## Decision

The TUI is rewritten on `@opentui/react` 0.8.1, with React 19 and `react-reconciler` 0.33, still
on Bun. It imports the pure modules of `src/renderer/src/lib/` as they are — `timeline`, `chat`,
`store`, `virtual`, `format` and `projects` — so a task reads the same in both apps and a fix to
how events become a conversation lands in both. The desktop app's React components are not
shared: they render DOM and Tailwind classes, and the TUI's render renderables. The JSX of
`tui/` compiles with `jsxImportSource: "@opentui/react"`, set in `tsconfig.tui.json` and in the
root `tsconfig.json` Bun reads.

Screen tests run under `bun test` on `@opentui/react/test-utils`' `testRender`, with simulated
keys, against a scripted API: the TUI's views take the API as a prop, so a test drives them with
no core and no Docker.

Rejected:

- **The imperative core API, kept.** Every screen would keep reimplementing what a reconciler
  does — diff the tree, keep focus and selection, unmount what left — and the 0.1 defects are
  that work done by hand.
- **`@opentui/solid`**, OpenCode's choice. Fine-grained reactivity suits a transcript, but it is
  a second component model in a repository whose renderer, tests and contributors are React's,
  and it shares nothing with `src/renderer` beyond the pure modules React shares as well.

## Consequences

- The TUI gains `@opentui/react` and `react-reconciler` as dependencies; React is already one.
  Its peers `react-devtools-core` and `ws` are not installed — `.npmrc`'s `legacy-peer-deps`
  skips them — and are loaded only when OpenTUI's `DEV` devtools are switched on, which the
  TUI never does; the binary build marks them external.
- `src/renderer/src/lib/` must stay free of DOM and of React DOM: it is now imported by a
  process that has neither.
- OpenTUI's React layer is as young as its core (0.x); an upgrade is a tested change, and the
  screen tests are what test it.
- Screen tests run under Bun rather than Vitest, so CI runs both and the gate sums them
  (plans/tui-revamp 1.5).

```

`docs/adr/0024-share-the-data-folder-between-processes.md`:

```md
---
status: accepted

# 0024 · Share the data folder between processes

## Context

plans/finish-the-harness 1.9 gave the data folder one lock, `hfr.lock`: the desktop app or the
terminal UI, never both, because `EventLog.recover()` marks every running task interrupted at
start and both container sweeps stop every running task container and sandbox — run under a live
app, either would wreck its tasks. plans/tui-revamp asks for the opposite: any number of TUIs,
each opened on its own folder, beside the desktop app, on one data folder. What the lock
protected has to be protected some other way, item by item:

- a task started in two apps at once, or one app's tasks recovered by another;
- the containers of another app's live tasks, stopped by a sweep;
- SQLite written by several processes: `SQLITE_BUSY`, and two apps migrating at once;
- an older app opening a database a newer one migrated;
- work that must happen once per machine, not once per app: the first-start upgrade that gives
  old tasks a project, the specialist's image build, the Claude sign-in;
- provider keys, which the desktop app encrypts with `safeStorage` into the database and the TUI
  keeps in the OS keychain through `Bun.secrets` — two stores neither app reads of the other;
- a view that only learns of a change through its own process's pushes.

adr:0017-keep-a-tasks-conversation-containers-and-files-until-it-is-deleted says starting the
app no longer removes stopped containers, and the sweeps only stop running ones; that holds.

## Decision

**The folder-wide lock goes; a lock per project replaces it.** `locks/project-<id>.lock` is
created exclusively and names the app, its pid and its start time. An app takes it when a task of
the project starts or reopens in it — a new task, a message or Continue on a closed one, a retry —
and holds it while any task of the project is open in that app, which is exactly while the
project's sandboxes are held (specs/projects R2.3); the last task to close releases it. Another
app is refused with the project's name and the app holding it. Reading, browsing and deciding on
a task's history need no lock: the desktop app lists every project and shows one held by another
app as taken by it. A lock whose process is gone is stale and taken over, as `hfr.lock` was.

**A process is identified by its pid and its start time**, recorded in a `processes` table with
the app's name and a heartbeat written every five seconds. A process is gone when its pid is not
alive, or its heartbeat is older than thirty seconds — which is what tells a reused pid from the
process that recorded it. A task records the process that opened it (`owner`).

**Recovery and both sweeps touch only what a gone process owned**, and run at the start of any
app: a task left running, waiting or stopped is interrupted only when its owner is gone; a running
task container is stopped only when its task's owner is gone; a running sandbox is stopped only
when no live process holds its project's lock.

**SQLite is shared, not guarded.** Every connection sets a five-second `busy_timeout`.
Migrations run inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, reading `user_version` again inside it, so two apps
starting together migrate once. Each migration records the app and version that ran it; a
database whose `user_version` is newer than the app knows is refused, before anything is written,
naming the app and version that migrated it.

**What happens once per machine is done once.** The first-start upgrade (`ProjectStore.adopt`)
runs in one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, so two apps on a fresh data folder produce one project
per source folder. The image build holds `locks/images.lock`: an app finding it held by a live
process reports the build as running in that app and reads the images' state again when it is
released, instead of building them a second time. The Claude sign-in holds `locks/login.lock`
while it runs, and a second app's sign-in is refused naming the app signing in. The Electron
single-instance lock stays: two desktop windows on one profile is not what this enables.

**An app learns of another process's changes by polling SQLite's `data_version`** every half
second — it changes only when another connection commits. On a change the app reads what moved
since its cursor — tasks, steps, patches and projects by `updated_at`, events by id, deletions by
absence — and pushes it to its view as if it had written it, so a view refreshes within one
second and needs no second channel. A key saved in one app bumps a `keys.rev` setting, and the
others read the keychain again.

**Provider keys live in one OS-keychain store both apps read**, through `@napi-rs/keyring`: one
generic credential per slot under the service `harness-for-rea`, its secret the key's UTF-8
bytes. It loads in Electron's Node and under Bun alike. `Bun.secrets` was the first choice for the
TUI and is not compatible: on Windows it writes a credential `@napi-rs/keyring` reads as empty,
and the desktop app cannot use it. At first start each app moves its old keys — the desktop app's
`safeStorage` settings, the TUI's `Bun.secrets` entries — into the shared store and removes them
where they were.

Rejected:

- **A lock per data folder that the TUI shares with other TUIs only.** Still one app at a time
  against the desktop app, which is the restriction being lifted.
- **A daemon owning the core, with the apps as clients.** One writer and no locks, but a third
  process to install, start, upgrade and keep alive, and a protocol between it and two views.
- **A file watcher on the database.** WAL writes land in `-wal` and `-shm`, notifications are
  unreliable across the platforms, and `data_version` answers the same question exactly.
- **Process start time read from the OS.** No portable call reaches it without spawning `ps` or
  PowerShell per check; the heartbeat answers liveness and pid reuse with one row.

## Consequences

- `hfr.lock`, `DataFolderBusy` and the TUI's "close the desktop app first" go; `tests/lock.test.ts`
  is rewritten for the per-project lock.
- A task can be read in one app while it runs in another; acting on it — a message, Continue,
  start over — is refused in the app that does not hold its project.
- Each app writes a heartbeat row every five seconds, and every app polls `data_version` twice a
  second: a cheap read that never touches the disk when nothing changed.
- An app that dies leaves its tasks running in the database until any app starts again: that
  app interrupts them and stops their containers. Live apps do not take over a dead app's tasks
  while they run.
- `@napi-rs/keyring` is a native module, the first in the stack: it ships prebuilt per platform
  as optional dependencies, needs no install script, and the TUI's binary build bundles the one
  for its target.
- A schema change now has a reader that can be older than the writer: the refusal names the newer
  app so the user knows which to update.

```

`docs/adr/0025-remove-the-containers-on-a-forced-stop.md`:

status: accepted
---

# 0025 · Remove the containers on a forced stop

## Context

adr:0017-keep-a-tasks-conversation-containers-and-files-until-it-is-deleted made cancelling, closing
and quitting stop a task's containers and keep them, so what a tool installed survives until the
task reopens. In use, a forced stop — a cancelled task, an app quit with tasks open, or an app
killed and swept at the next start — leaves stopped containers piling up in `docker ps -a`, one per
task and per sandbox, though nothing of the task's lives only in them: adr:0017 already put every
file a task writes under `tasks/<id>/` on the host, bound into the containers, and the conversation
in SQLite. The user asked for the instances to go on a forced stop, with the task kept.

## Decision

A forced stop removes the containers; an ordinary end keeps them stopped.

- **Forced**: cancelling a task, quitting the app with a task open, and the start-up sweep of the
  containers a gone process left running (adr:0024-share-the-data-folder-between-processes). The
  task container is removed (`docker rm -f`); the project's sandboxes are removed once no task of
  the project is open, their records kept.
- **Ordinary**: closing a conversation, and the end of a turn. The containers are stopped and kept,
  as adr:0017 has it, so installed tools survive the common case of coming back to a task.

Nothing of the task is lost either way: `/scratch`, each sandbox's `/work` and `/root/out`, the
delegations' workspaces and the conversation's checkpoints stay, and a reopened task creates the
containers again over the same folders and tells the orchestrator that what was installed is gone —
the path adr:0017 already takes when Docker has lost a container.

Rejected: removing on every end, which loses installed tools on each close; keeping on every end,
which is what piled up.

## Consequences

- After a cancel, a quit or a crash, a reopened task starts on fresh containers and reinstalls
  what it needs; its files are where they were.
- `docker ps -a` holds stopped containers only for tasks closed in the ordinary way.
- adr:0017 holds for files, conversation and the ordinary end; this record amends only what a
  forced stop does to the containers.

```

`docs/adr/0026-proxy-host-engines-to-the-agents-as-mcp-integrations.md`:

---
status: accepted
---

# 0026 · Proxy host engines to the agents as MCP integrations

## Context

The user wants the agents to use engines that only run on the Windows host: Cheat Engine now, to
analyse the live memory of Windows software, and IDA Pro's MCP later. Cheat Engine's MCP is to be
built on `miscusi-peek/cheatengine-mcp-bridge` (MIT). The user wants the integrations as a list
in Settings, and to choose tool by tool which go to the orchestrator and which to the specialist:
by default the specialist gets every tool and the orchestrator only what lets it discover what is
there before it delegates.

The specialist runs in a Linux container per delegation
(adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task) with REA as its analysis server
(adr:0018-make-rea-native-to-the-specialist); the orchestrator plans and delegates
(adr:0011-limit-the-orchestrator-to-planning-delegation-and-its-own-code). The upstream bridge is
a Lua script inside Cheat Engine answering JSON-RPC on a named pipe, a Python MCP server on the
host and an optional TCP relay for a server in a container. Its Lua answers about 180 commands —
memory writes, DLL injection, code execution, a kernel driver, shell and file commands — to any
client of the pipe; the gate on the shell commands is in the Python server only. A container
reaches a service bound to the host's `127.0.0.1` through `host.docker.internal`, checked on this
host's Docker Desktop, and the sandboxes have full internet access
(adr:0013-give-the-sandboxes-full-internet-access), so a relay would hand Cheat Engine to every
process in every container, a sample's code included. What a target's memory or database holds is
the target's data, and text in it reaches the model.

## Decision

The app carries a list of integrations in its own code, each with its settings, its checks, its
catalog of tools, the orchestrator's default for each tool and, when its tools work on one, its
kind of target; Settings offers no way to add another server. The app is the only path to an
engine. The specialist gets one MCP server per integration, offering the tools checked for it,
whose calls travel as files over the existing ask channel
(adr:0008-ask-the-user-from-the-specialist-over-the-run-channel) to the app; the orchestrator gets
the tools checked for it as its own tools, under the same names. The app checks every call
against the catalog, the agent's checkboxes and the task's approved target before it forwards it.
A target — Cheat Engine's is a process by PID — is approved by the user every time, in an
automatic task too, with no approval by default. No mount, port or environment variable is added
to the container. For Cheat Engine the app ships its own bridge, derived from upstream commit
`6bd7ce90`, on its own pipe, with only the handlers of commands that read. Rejected: the upstream
TCP relay, which needs no credential and is reachable from every container; the upstream Python
server, which adds Python to the host and leaves its Lua answering every command; MCP servers the
user adds, whose tools the app could not gate by kind; a mount of its own for the calls, which
widens the boundary when the ask channel already crosses it; and the container's servers in the
base image, which would need a GHCR publish and a re-pin
(adr:0012-pull-the-specialists-base-image-from-ghcr) for every catalog change.

## Consequences

- This extends adr:0011's allowlist with the tools the user checks for the orchestrator. Its
  defaults keep the rule that analysis goes to the specialist; a user who checks a tool that reads
  a target gives the orchestrator's model — a cheap one, on a provider of the user's choice — the
  target's data and any injection in it, with a warning and nothing more.
- The specialist can read anything the approved target exposes, secrets included, and what it
  reads goes to its model and its report. The approval is the only check on which target that is.
- Anything in the container can write a call file, so a sample's code can use the specialist's
  tools on the approved target; it cannot name another target or a tool off the catalog.
- The system prompt names an integration's answers as data, which is policy, not a boundary.
- Cheat Engine's bridge is a fork of a 6,000-line Lua file: upstream fixes come in by hand, and a
  test that holds its handlers equal to the catalog is what stops a write command slipping back.
- An engine runs with the user's rights on the host and answers only while it is open with its
  plugin loaded; nothing in the app sandboxes the engine itself.
- Writes, injection, breakpoints and debugging stay out of Cheat Engine's catalog; adding any of
  them is a new decision.
- Containers can still reach other services on the host's loopback; that is a separate decision
  this record does not take.

```

`docs/glossary.md`:

```md
# Glossary

One canonical term per concept, and the synonyms nobody should use for it. Domain
vocabulary drifts by default — three names for one thing appear within a week of two
people working in parallel — so this file picks the name and the rest become
findings.

One entry per line:

```markdown
- **order total** — the amount charged, in minor units. Avoid: grand total, sum
```

The term is bold, the definition follows an em dash, and `Avoid:` lists the
synonyms it replaces, comma-separated and optional. Every synonym listed here is
reported wherever it appears as a whole word under `docs/`, so list one only when
you mean it.

Reach for the `glossary` skill when a term is coined, contested, or renamed. Define
what the thing *is*, not what it is called, and do not define what is obvious to
anyone in the domain.

<!-- Entries go below this line. Delete the guidance above once they read for
themselves. -->

- **orchestrator** — the DeepAgents agent on a model from OpenRouter, DeepSeek or another OpenAI-compatible provider that plans a task, delegates steps and consolidates the results. Avoid: coordinator, planner agent
- **specialist** — the Claude Opus agent run through the pinned Claude Code CLI for steps that need deep analysis. Avoid: expert agent, worker agent
- **delegation** — handing one step from the orchestrator to the specialist with a context package. Avoid: handoff
- **context package** — what a delegation carries: the orchestrator's brief, objective, files and excerpts, environment facts, questions, constraints, and the expected report format. Avoid: context bundle
- **brief** — the orchestrator's own technical prompt to the specialist inside a context package: what the artifact is, what is known about it and what one step must discover, never the user's request or purpose (adr:0019-keep-the-specialists-brief-technical). Avoid: narrative, pretext
- **sandbox** — the container the specialist runs in, with `workspace/<uuid>/` holding copies of only the files it was given mounted at `/work`: one the orchestrator created and prepared (`hfr-sbx-<id>`), or a delegation's own
- **evidence** — a claim in a report tied to a file and line range, or to a captured tool output, that the orchestrator can check
- **event** — one normalized, redacted record of an agent action, stored in SQLite and shown in the UI
- **patch approval** — the user's explicit decision to apply a change produced in the sandbox to the original files
- **task** — one request from the user in a project, run by the orchestrator from start to its consolidated answer. Avoid: job
- **step** — one unit of a task: a todo the orchestrator wrote, or a delegation
- **workspace** — `workspace/<uuid>/` under the app's data folder, the copies a delegation's sandbox mounts at `/work`, with its snapshot and run directory beside it
- **base image** — `hfr-specialist-base` on GHCR: the specialist image without Claude Code, pinned by digest in `sandbox/images.json`
- **specialist image** — `hfr-specialist:<version>`, built locally from the base image plus the verified Claude Code CLI
- **project** — a target with a goal, a model and its tasks, which share the project's sandboxes and analyses (adr:0020-group-tasks-into-projects-that-share-their-analyses)
- **target** — the file or folder a project analyses: a file is copied into the project's folder, a folder is read in place
- **analysis** — a delegation's report with its evidence, kept with the project so every later task of it can read it
- **safeguard refusal** — the specialist declining a step under its usage policy: its own state, never a failure to retry or a request to reword
- **unknowns ledger** — the project's list of what an analysis left open, each item tied to the analysis that raised it and the one that closed it
- **test vector** — an input and the output the target produced for it, recorded by an analysis and replayed against a reimplementation
- **chat timeline** — the task view: each agent's turns, tool calls and delegations, the specialist's own tool calls nested under its delegation
- **TUI** — the terminal UI on OpenTUI under Bun, beside the desktop app
- **MCP integration** — an engine on the user's machine, such as Cheat Engine, that the app carries in its own list and the agents reach only through the app, each of its tools checked per agent in Settings (adr:0026-proxy-host-engines-to-the-agents-as-mcp-integrations). Avoid: connector, custom MCP server
- **integration target** — what an MCP integration's tools work on, such as one Windows process by pid for Cheat Engine, approved by the user in every task; not a project's target. Avoid: attached process
- **bridge** — the app's read-only Lua script in Cheat Engine's autorun folder, derived from the upstream cheatengine-mcp-bridge, answering the app on its own named pipe. Avoid: CE script

```

`docs/notes.md`:

```md
# Notes

Every small durable observation about this project, one per line. The gotcha, the
why-not, the "careful, this looks wrong and is not" — the things that used to be a
comment beside the code, where only the reader already looking at that line ever
found them.

**Notes do not live in the code.** A comment says what a thing is and how to use
it; anything else is a note, and it belongs here with the path it is about
attached to it.

One note is one line, index fields first:

```markdown
- n-0000 2026-02-09 #gotcha @internal/cli/launch.go — wrap writes MCP config to the agent's own file, so it outlives the session
```

`n-0000` is the id; real ones start at `n-0001` and are never reused, so a note can
be cited as `n-0042` from anywhere — including the one place code may still mention
one. Then the date. Then `#tags`, at least one, which is what the log is queried by.
Then `@paths`, repo-relative, which is what keeps a note attached to the code without
living inside it. Then an em dash, and the note itself.

The one line is the contract: a match is a whole note, never a fragment of one, so
`grep ' #gotcha ' docs/notes.md` and `scc notes find --tag gotcha` answer the same
question. Write with `scc notes add "…" --tag gotcha --path <path>`, which
allocates the id and gets the format right; read with `scc notes find`,
`scc notes tags`, `scc notes show n-0001`.

**If it needs a second line, it is not a note.** Something learned and worth
explaining is a `wiki/` page. A decision that is hard to reverse is an `adr/`
record. Something that has to be done is a task in a plan. A note is the thing
none of those three would take.

over this file answers with the example above as well as with the notes. -->

`docs/stack.md`:

```md
# Stack

Every adopted technology, with one line on why it earned its place. **Technology
that is not listed here is an open decision, never something adopted silently** —
and because this project's dependency file is structured data rather than source,
that rule is checkable: a direct dependency declared there and absent from here is
reported.

So adding a dependency is a two-step act: add it, and say here why.

```markdown
## Runtime

- **the-http-router** — routing with the standard library's handler contract, no
  framework underneath it.

## Development

- **the-test-runner** — what CI runs; the suite is the gate for a feature.
```

Group however the project actually thinks about it. What matters is that the name
appears and the reason is one line a reader can disagree with.

themselves. -->

## Runtime

- **Electron** — desktop shell with a Node main process that can spawn and supervise the Claude Code CLI; same base as `study-lab` and the MagnoTech desktop app.
- **electron-vite** — one build for main, preload and renderer, carried over from `study-lab`.
- **TypeScript** — one typed contract shared by main, preload and renderer.
- **React** — renderer UI, as in both reference projects.
- **Tailwind CSS** (with **@tailwindcss/vite**) — renderer styling, as in `study-lab`, themed through shadcn/ui's CSS variables.
- **shadcn/ui** on **radix-ui** — the renderer's components, copied in as source on Radix primitives for keyboard, focus and ARIA behaviour ([adr:0010-build-the-renderer-on-shadcn-ui-and-radix]).
- **class-variance-authority**, **clsx** and **tailwind-merge** — the shadcn/ui helpers for variant classes and merging utilities.
- **lucide-react** — icons, as in `study-lab`.
- **react-markdown** with **remark-gfm** — the conversation's messages and reports as GitHub-flavoured markdown in the desktop app, raw HTML never interpreted (specs/chat R7.6).
- **mdast-util-from-markdown**, **mdast-util-gfm** and **micromark-extension-gfm** — the same markdown parsed to a tree the TUI draws, so both apps read a message alike.
- **@types/mdast** — the types of that tree.
- **Lezer** (`@lezer/highlight`, `@lezer/common` and the `@lezer/javascript`, `python`, `json`, `cpp`, `rust`, `java`, `go`, `html`, `css`, `xml` and `yaml` parsers) — CodeMirror's incremental parsers, coloring the code in a message for both apps from one palette, with no WASM and no DOM.
- **node:sqlite** — built into the Node that Electron bundles, so no native module to rebuild; holds tasks, steps and events ([adr:0005-store-events-in-sqlite-with-raw-jsonl-per-task]).
- **deepagents** — orchestration: planning, delegation tools, filesystem backends and approval interrupts ([adr:0001-use-deepagents-on-openrouter-for-orchestration]).
- **@langchain/openai** — the OpenAI chat client behind the DeepSeek and custom orchestrator providers, which only need a base URL and a key ([adr:0014-add-openai-compatible-orchestrator-providers]); already installed beneath DeepAgents and `@langchain/openrouter`.
- **langchain** — `todoListMiddleware`, which DeepAgents 1.15 no longer adds by default and which provides `write_todos`.
- **@langchain/langgraph** — `MemorySaver` and `Command`, the checkpointer and resume command behind patch approval.
- **langsmith** — a peer dependency of DeepAgents; nothing is sent to LangSmith.
- **@langchain/openrouter** and **@langchain/core** — `ChatOpenRouter`, the model DeepAgents runs on, so the orchestrator is not tied to one vendor.
- **zod** — runtime validation of IPC arguments and tool schemas at the trust boundary.
- **Claude Code CLI (pinned binary)** — the specialist, verified by the signed release manifest and SHA-256 at image build, not an npm dependency ([adr:0002-run-the-specialist-through-the-pinned-claude-code-cli]).
- **Docker** with **node:24.22.2-bookworm-slim** (pinned by digest) — the specialist's base image, one container per delegation ([adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task]); Node runs the ask-user MCP server ([adr:0008-ask-the-user-from-the-specialist-over-the-run-channel]) and the orchestrator's own scripts in `/scratch`. The verifying build stage stays on **debian:bookworm-slim**.
- **Bun** — the TUI's runtime: OpenTUI needs it, and the core runs on it unchanged, `node:sqlite` included ([adr:0022-run-the-tui-on-bun-with-opentui]).
- **OpenTUI** (`@opentui/core`) — the TUI's renderer, a native terminal UI core driven from TypeScript ([adr:0022-run-the-tui-on-bun-with-opentui]).
- **@opentui/react** with **react-reconciler** — the TUI's React layer over OpenTUI, so its screens are declarative and share `src/renderer/src/lib` with the desktop app ([adr:0023-build-the-tui-on-opentuis-react-layer]); its peers `react-devtools-core` and `ws`, which `legacy-peer-deps` does not install, are only loaded by OpenTUI's devtools and stay out.
- **@napi-rs/keyring** — the one OS-keychain store both apps read provider keys from, prebuilt per platform with no install script ([adr:0024-share-the-data-folder-between-processes]).
- **web-tree-sitter** — OpenTUI's required peer, which `.npmrc`'s `legacy-peer-deps` does not install by itself; the TUI's binary and package carry it.
- **GitHub Container Registry** — hosts the specialist's base image, everything but Claude Code, published by the Images workflow and pulled by digest ([adr:0012-pull-the-specialists-base-image-from-ghcr]).
- **Cheat Engine** (on the user's Windows machine, not shipped) — the first MCP integration: the agents read a live process's memory through it, only through the app ([adr:0026-proxy-host-engines-to-the-agents-as-mcp-integrations]).
- **The bridge** (`sandbox/cheat-engine/hfr-bridge.lua`) — the app's own read-only fork of `miscusi-peek/cheatengine-mcp-bridge` (MIT) at commit `6bd7ce90`, its write, injection, execution and debugging handlers deleted; upstream fixes come in by hand ([adr:0026-proxy-host-engines-to-the-agents-as-mcp-integrations]).

## Development

- **Vitest** with V8 coverage (**@vitest/coverage-v8**) — the delivery gate reads a coverage figure, which `node:test` in `study-lab` does not produce.
- **Vite** and **@vitejs/plugin-react** — what electron-vite builds the renderer with.
- **@types/node**, **@types/react**, **@types/react-dom** — types for the TypeScript build.
- **oxlint** — the lint layer, as in the MagnoTech desktop app.
- **Prettier** — formatting, as in the MagnoTech desktop app.
- **electron-builder** — Windows NSIS installer.

```

# Wiki

The entry point. Every page under `wiki/pages/` has to be reachable from here —
directly, or through a page that is — because a page nothing links to is a page
nobody will find again.

Pages link to each other as `[[page-slug]]`, where the slug is the filename without
its extension and without its directory. A link that resolves to no page is reported,
and so is a page this index cannot reach.

This file and `changelog.md` live here rather than in `pages/`: they are the wiki's
fixed documents, not pages, and neither is ever an orphan.

`docs/wiki/pages/craft-anything.md`:

```md
# craft-anything

[storytold/craft-anything](https://github.com/storytold/craft-anything) is a Rust desktop
app, CLI and MCP server (early alpha, MIT OR Apache-2.0) that studies a website, app or game,
has a coding agent rebuild it, and checks the rebuild against the original. It is the nearest
public relative of this harness: its builder is also Claude Code, driven with `claude -p`. It
differs on who does what. There, one agent analyses and builds; here, the split
between orchestrator and specialist keeps the analysis with the specialist and the code with
the orchestrator (adr:0011-limit-the-orchestrator-to-planning-delegation-and-its-own-code).

## How it works

A run has four stages (`crates/ai/src/rebuild/mod.rs`):

1. **Study.** No model is involved. It triages the target, prepares Ghidra and, for a console
   program, runs the original on fixed inputs. It writes `capture/README.md` for the builder.
2. **Build.** The user's local `claude -p` runs on the host, with the project folder as its
   working folder, craft-anything's MCP server attached, and an approval tool. The prompt
   rules are in `brief.rs`.
3. **Check.** Pluggable checks score the rebuild:
   - it builds;
   - it prints and exits like the original for each captured input;
   - every value in `app/mechanics.json` carries a `source` (function address or evidence
     id) or `estimated: true`, and every sourced number appears in the code as written.

   Missing evidence never counts as a pass (`crates/engine/src/workspace.rs`).
4. **Refine.** The first failing check goes back to the builder. This stops after six rounds,
   or once 90% of the checks pass.

The builder keeps an **unknowns ledger** (`crates/evidence/src/unknown.rs`). Each entry holds
a question, its severity, the probes tried, evidence for and against, and a resolution. The
builder must record a gap before guessing, and the final status counts what is still open.

## What it suggests for this harness

The ideas below are ranked by value. Ideas carry no license obligation. Prompt text copied
word for word would need the MIT notice.

- **Evidence that points into a binary.** Let a report cite a function address or an REA
  evidence id as well as `path:lines`. Today `parseEvidence` in `src/shared/context.ts` drops
  anything that is not `path:<line>` without saying so.
- **A machine-readable contract at the end of a report.** List functions with inputs, outputs
  and side effects; constants, each with a source or `estimated: true`; and test vectors. The
  app can then check that each sourced constant reaches the orchestrator's code, instead of a
  cheap model extracting them from prose.
- **Vectors observed, not inferred.** The specialist runs the original in its sandbox and
  records input/output pairs. A tool replays them against the reimplementation. Re-delegation
  stops after a bounded number of rounds.
- **A task-scoped unknowns ledger.** Open questions carry over into each new context package
  and appear in the final answer. REA's own `record_unknown` can feed it.
- **A reminder when the orchestrator concludes without delegating.** This is the fallback
  adr:0011 says instructions alone lack.
- **Evidence discipline in the specialist's prompt.** Missing evidence is never proof. Mark a
  value estimated only after looking for it. Record each open question with what would settle
  it.

## What does not fit

These parts conflict with how the harness is built:

- Running `claude` on the host breaks the container boundary of
  adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task.
- One agent that analyses and builds breaks the split of adr:0011.
- Edits allowed without approval break patch approval.

These parts are off purpose:

- its asset and likeness checks;
- the 284-tool engine, which REA covers here ([[rea-in-the-sandbox]]).

```

`docs/wiki/pages/rea-in-the-sandbox.md`:

```md
# REA in the specialist's sandbox

## What REA is

REA ("Reverse Engineer Anything", [morluto/rea](https://github.com/morluto/rea), `rea-agents` on npm,
MIT) is a local reverse engineering CLI and MCP server. Version 6.8.0 has one catalog of 229 tools
covering:

- native binaries;
- .NET assemblies;
- JavaScript and Electron applications;
- archives and packages;
- Android APKs;
- firmware;
- captures and browsers.

Every result is an immutable Evidence record. The skill `reverse-engineer-anything` is the workflow
that tells an agent how to use them. REA's own `AGENTS.md` is a contributor guide, not agent
instructions: the skill and the server's MCP prompts are the only agent guidance it ships.

## How it runs headless in the container

**Install.** REA is installed globally at a pinned version: `npm install -g rea-agents@<v>`, on
Node `^24.22.1`, with no install scripts. The 6.8.0 tarball carries no shrinkwrap: direct
dependencies are exact, transitive ones float.

**Connection.** The specialist reaches it through `--mcp-config` as a stdio server: `node <npm
root>/rea-agents/scripts/rea.mjs mcp`. Its tools appear as `mcp__rea__<tool>`.

**Never `rea setup`.** It writes a client registration and a personal skill copy, and the specialist
loads neither, because it starts with `--setting-sources ""` and `--strict-mcp-config`. The skill
therefore reaches the specialist through its system prompt. The whole skill directory has to be in
the image, its `references/` included, so the specialist can read them. The server also serves the
skill at run time (`search_guidance`, `read_guidance_section`) and six guided workflows as MCP
prompts.

**What works.** REA installs no engines. On Linux it needs a procps `ps` for every child it
supervises. What works headless follows from what the image supplies:

- **Built in:** JavaScript, Electron and ASAR; archive inventory; PE, ELF and Mach-O inspectors;
  Go, Rust, pyc, BEAM, EVM, IL2CPP metadata, SQLite; .NET metadata and CIL.
- **With a supplied tool:**
  - Ghidra 12.1 with JDK 21 (`GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR`, `JAVA_HOME`); Debian bookworm ships only JDK 17;
  - JADX (`REA_JADX_MCP_JAR`), Apktool (`REA_APKTOOL_COMMAND`);
  - WABT, Binwalk and Unblob, tshark, objdump, GDB, Rizin;
  - Chromium for browser capture.
- **Unavailable:**
  - Hopper, JEB and IDA, which are commercial or licence-bound;
  - Apple native UI and LLDB tools, which need macOS;
  - ADB tools, which need a device;
  - Frida, whose optional binding is not installed.

`binary_session {}` is the authority on what a server can do; its `tool_availability` says why each
unavailable operation is unavailable.

**Cost and timeouts.** The catalog is large. `REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact` (the default)
and a `REA_MCP_TOOL_FAMILIES` subset keep it from crowding the context, which matters when the
model endpoint turns tool search off. Ghidra's cold start can take 330 s, so the client's tool
timeout has to allow it.

**State.** State lives under `~/.rea`, which the XDG variables do not move.

## Workflow and evidence model

**Routing and sessions.** Route the target first: the input decides the first tool. An ASAR goes to
`analyze_javascript_application`, an APK to `inspect_android_package`, a .NET assembly to
`inspect_managed_artifact`, firmware to `inspect_firmware_regions`, a native file to `open_binary`.
`open_binary` binds one active target per server until `close_binary`.

**Summary first.** Ask for `detail: "summary"`, then page the retained record with
`inspect_analysis_view` and its `parent_evidence_id`. Never repeat an identical analysis.

**Evidence records.** Every record carries an `evidence_id` of the form `ev_<64 hex>`, a SHA-256 of
its canonical content. With it come:

- the subject's SHA-256;
- the provider;
- an authority: `shipped-artifact`, `controlled-replay`, `historical-reference`,
  `external-service` or `analyst-inference`;
- a confidence: `observed`, `derived` or `inferred`;
- its limitations and coverage.

Static evidence never establishes execution.

**Unknowns.** An open question is a residual unknown, `unk_<64 hex>`:

- `record_unknown` creates it with its supporting and contradicting evidence.
- `update_unknown` revises it against its current revision; on a conflict, read it again rather
  than retrying.
- `verify_unknown_resolution` confirms that a `verified` resolution is backed by qualifying
  evidence.

**Keeping an investigation.** The evidence ledger lives in the server process's memory, so
`export_evidence_bundle` is the only way an investigation outlives the specialist.
`import_evidence_bundle` brings one back.

**Reconstruction.** `build_reconstruction_obligation_ledger` turns a bundle into obligations. Each
closes only with a unique owner, fixtures and a passing verifier of comparable authority. A pass of
`verify_reconstruction` covers only the claims it declares.

## What the specialist's operating guide says

- REA is already connected and its tools are fixed. Never run `rea setup`, `rea update` or `npx
  rea-agents`, and never ask for a client restart. The skill's "connect only when needed" section
  does not apply.
- Call `binary_session {}` once, then route the target and work summary-first.
- Turn the objective into a checklist of questions. Keep a finding ledger: each conclusion with its
  Evidence IDs, authority and confidence, and what remains unknown.
- Record every unresolved question with `record_unknown`. Before calling one resolved, run
  `verify_unknown_resolution`.
- Label each claim as observation, inference or unknown, and cite `ev_…` and `unk_…` IDs verbatim.
- Before finishing:
  - export the evidence bundle to the output folder;
  - close the target;
  - mark each checklist question answered, partial or unresolved.

Related: [[craft-anything]], whose unknowns ledger and sourced-constant check rest on the same idea.

```

`docs/wiki/pages/tui-0-1-defects.md`:

```md
# tui-0-1-defects

The terminal UI shipped in 0.1 (`tui/src/app.ts`, `tui/src/view.ts`, specs/tui) walked through
the first-run setup, a project, a long task, a question and a safeguard refusal beside the
desktop app on the same machine, and read against the renderer's views. Each defect carries the
steps that show it; each parity gap names the API method the desktop app's views call that the
0.1 TUI never reaches. The revamp (plans/tui-revamp.md) fixes them, and each spec that does
links back here.

## Defects

1. **The folder it is run in is ignored.** Run `harness-for-rea` inside a sample's folder: it
   opens the projects list, never the folder, and `harness-for-rea C:\samples\x` is not
   accepted. Fixed by specs/tui-launch.
2. **Only one app on the data folder.** Open the desktop app, then run the TUI: it prints
   "already open in the desktop app" and exits — and the reverse holds. Two TUIs in two
   folders cannot run either. Fixed by specs/shared-data-folder.
3. **One single-line input for everything.** A request cannot span lines, there is no history
   (Up does nothing), and the line means a command, an answer or a message depending on the
   screen and on whether a question waits — typing a reply while a question arrives answers
   the question. Fixed by specs/tui-shell and specs/tui-conversation.
4. **The whole timeline is redrawn as one plain-text block on every event.** Start a long
   task: each event rebuilds every line, scrolling back jumps to the bottom on the next event,
   markdown shows raw (`**`, fences), and code is not highlighted. Fixed by
   specs/tui-conversation.
5. **Tool calls and delegations cannot be opened.** A run of tool calls is one summary line
   and a delegation is its title plus the specialist's one-line entries: the context package,
   the report, the evidence and the files copied, read and written are nowhere. Fixed by
   specs/tui-conversation.
6. **A gated tool call is invisible.** The timeline skips the `approval` block, so a task
   waiting on a decision shows nothing to decide and stalls. Fixed by specs/tui-conversation.
7. **Lists lose their place.** On the projects or a project's screen, every `task` push
   refetches the screen and reassigns the list's options, so the selection jumps back to the
   top while another task runs; on a project's screen pushes of other projects' tasks
   refetch it too. Fixed by specs/tui-shell.
8. **Tab between a list and the input is the only navigation.** On a project's screen, text
   typed while the list was meant to have focus starts a task. Escape does nothing on the
   setup and projects screens. Fixed by specs/tui-shell.
9. **Ctrl+C quits at once.** Pressed during a running turn it stops every task of the app
   without asking. Fixed by specs/tui-shell (Ctrl+C twice, Esc to interrupt).
10. **Errors vanish.** An error goes to the status line, and the next redraw replaces it with
    the screen's help text. Fixed by specs/tui-shell (toasts).
11. **Creating a project needs a command grammar.** `/new <name> | <goal> | <target path>`,
    with no detection of the target's kind and no prefill from the Settings model. Fixed by
    specs/tui-launch and specs/tui-panels.
12. **The setup cannot finish without the desktop app's help.** `/login` prints the sign-in
    URL but never opens the browser; a sign-in cannot be cancelled and Claude cannot be signed
    out; the image build shows no log; `/key` sets the current provider's key with no way to
    pick a provider or a base URL, and `/model` takes an id with no list to pick from. Fixed
    by specs/tui-panels.
13. **Nothing after the setup can be changed.** No settings: provider, model, efforts,
    timeouts. Fixed by specs/tui-panels.
14. **A task's working state is a word.** The header shows `[running]`: no elapsed time, no
    tokens, no cost, no plan. Fixed by specs/tui-conversation and specs/tui-panels.

## Parity gaps

The desktop app's views call 36 API methods; the 0.1 TUI reaches 18. Not reached:

| Method | Where the desktop app calls it | Fixed by |
|---|---|---|
| `decidePatch` | a patch's approve and reject | specs/tui-conversation |
| `decideTool` | a gated tool call's approve, edit and reject | specs/tui-conversation |
| `closeTask` | Close on a task | specs/tui-conversation |
| `deleteTask` | Delete on a task | specs/tui-conversation |
| `retryTask` | Start over on an interrupted, failed or cancelled task | specs/tui-conversation |
| `listTasks` | the sidebar's recent tasks | specs/tui-launch (`--resume`) |
| `deleteProject` | the project overview | specs/tui-panels |
| `detectTarget` | the new-project dialog | specs/tui-launch |
| `pickTarget`, `pickFolder` | the new-project dialog's pickers | specs/tui-launch (typed paths) |
| `sandboxStatus` | the setup's image step and its banner | specs/tui-panels |
| `loginStatus` | the setup's sign-in step | specs/tui-panels |
| `openLoginUrl` | the sign-in's Open button | specs/tui-panels |
| `cancelLogin` | the sign-in's Cancel | specs/tui-panels |
| `logout` | the sign-in's Sign out | specs/tui-panels |
| `keyStatus` | the provider step | specs/tui-panels |
| `clearKey` | the provider step's Remove | specs/tui-panels |
| `listModels` | the model picker | specs/tui-panels |

The task view's event log, its usage per agent and the project's analyses and unknowns are
shown by the desktop app from data the TUI already fetches and never draws.

```

`electron.vite.config.ts`:

```ts
import { resolve } from "path"
import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/vite"
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react"
import { defineConfig } from "electron-vite"
import type { Plugin } from "vite"
import { contentSecurityPolicy } from "./src/main/csp"

/** The built page carries its CSP as a meta tag: a file:// page gets no response headers. */
const csp: Plugin = {
  name: "hfr-csp",
  apply: "build",
  transformIndexHtml: (html) =>
    html.replace(
      "<head>",
      `<head>
    <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="${contentSecurityPolicy()}" />`,
    ),
}

const shared = resolve(__dirname, "src/shared")

export default defineConfig({
  main: {
    resolve: { alias: { "@shared": shared } },
    build: { rollupOptions: { external: ["node:sqlite"] } },
  },
  preload: {
    resolve: { alias: { "@shared": shared } },
  },
  renderer: {
    plugins: [react(), tailwindcss(), csp],
    resolve: {
      alias: {
        "@": resolve(__dirname, "src/renderer/src"),
        "@shared": shared,
      },
    },
  },
})

# Ci pr gate

CI runs on pull requests only, and `main` takes a change only through a pull request whose
build, format, lint and tests passed.

## Why

CI ran on every push to `main` and on pull requests, but nothing stopped a merge or a direct
push to `main` while it was red. The user asked that a change reach `main` only when its tests
pass.

## Paths

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — the `gate` job and its triggers
- GitHub branch protection of `main` — the required `gate` check

## References

- `.claude/rules/delivery.md` — every change lands through a pull request

## Out of scope

- Requiring a review approval before a merge
- Running `scc validate` in CI; the pre-push hook runs it locally
- The Images workflow, which publishes the base image on its own triggers

## Tasks

- [x] 1.1 (Unit) Run the CI gate on pull requests only, one run per pull request at a time
- [x] 1.2 (Unit) Protect `main`: require the `gate` check, up to date with `main`, for administrators too
  _Depends 1.1_

## Done when

- A pull request into `main` shows the `gate` check, and GitHub refuses its merge while the check is red or pending
- A direct push to `main` is refused

```

# Finish the harness

Everything still pending for Harness for REA after projects and onboarding: a chat timeline that
holds long runs, a specialist whose questions and refusals never stall a task, the terminal UI and
its release to GitHub and npm, the README, and the Craft Anything ideas that make an analysis
checkable.

## Why

Long tasks freeze the task view, every specialist question waits on the user even when the
orchestrator could answer it, a safeguard refusal looks like any other failure, and the app only
runs from source on one desktop. The work is done when a long task's history scrolls within a
frame budget, questions are answered by the orchestrator first and refusals wait on the user's
choice, the desktop app and the CLI/TUI ship from a manual release on `main` for Windows x64 and
macOS arm64/x64 with the CLI on npm, and an analysis carries a contract, an unknowns ledger and
replayable test vectors.

## Paths

- `src/renderer/src/views/TaskView.tsx`, `src/renderer/src/lib/chat.ts`, `src/renderer/src/lib/store.ts`, `src/renderer/src/components/chat/`
- `src/main/events/log.ts`, `src/main/index.ts`, `src/main/credentials.ts`, `src/shared/api.ts`, `src/shared/types.ts`
- `src/main/delegation.ts`, `src/main/orchestrator/`, `src/main/sandbox/docker.ts`, `sandbox/specialist/`
- `tui/`, `.github/workflows/release.yml`, `electron-builder.yml`, `package.json`, `docs/stack.md`, `docs/adr/`, `README.md`

## References

- `specs/chat-timeline/` — the task view as a chat timeline in the style of Claude Code Web and Codex Web: each agent's turns, tool calls and delegations, the specialist's tool calls nested under its delegation; newest events first through a `before` cursor with older pages on demand, scroll anchored when a page is prepended, only what is near the viewport rendered, events folded incrementally, usage and step state read from the main process rather than from the loaded page, payloads collapsed until opened; deltas to `specs/desktop-ui/` R2.2 and `specs/event-log/` for paged reads in both directions
- `specs/specialist-lifecycle/` — owned by this plan, and the spec plans/specialist-rea.md also names: a specialist question answered by one call to the orchestrator's model with the delegation's context, and put to the user only when it needs a fact only the user has; a safeguard refusal as its own state with its own event kind, distinct from the app's `sandbox.refused`, told to the orchestrator, where the user stops the task, skips the step, or asks for a different technical approach, never a reworded request nor a purpose added to the brief; the specialist container's removal and the Opus pin verified
- `specs/analysis-contract/` — the specialist's report as a JSON contract the orchestrator validates, a report that fails it returned to the specialist, and an unknowns ledger per project whose open items reach the next task's context package
- `specs/vector-replay/` — test vectors an analysis records, replayed in the sandbox against a reimplementation to check it behaves as the target does
- `specs/tui/` — a terminal UI on OpenTUI beside the Electron app, on the core shared with it behind interfaces for its Electron-only parts, the provider key entered once and kept in the OS keychain, the first-run setup and projects adapted to the terminal, and refusing to start while the desktop app holds the data folder, as the desktop app refuses while the TUI does
- `specs/release/` — a manually dispatched workflow on `main` that builds the desktop app and the CLI/TUI for Windows x64, macOS arm64 and macOS x64, unsigned with the macOS first-run workaround documented, publishes them to GitHub Releases, and publishes the CLI to npmjs with its token as a repository secret

`plans/harness-for-rea.md`:

```md
---
autonomy: auto
ci: wait

# harness-for-rea

A desktop app where an orchestrator model on OpenRouter decomposes a software
engineering task and delegates deep analysis to a Claude Opus specialist running
in Claude Code, each delegation in its own read-only sandbox, with every event
logged and visible in real time.

## Why

Legacy-system comprehension, debugging and authorized reverse engineering need
deep reasoning on narrow, well-scoped evidence, while planning and consolidation
can run on any model the user picks. The app makes that split explicit, keeps the
specialist away from everything outside its task, and leaves an audit trail of who
read and changed what. Done means a user can describe a task, watch it decompose
and delegate, inspect the evidence, and approve or reject any proposed change.

## Paths

- `src/main/` — orchestrator, specialist, sandbox, events, credentials
- `src/preload/`, `src/shared/` — typed, validated IPC contract
- `src/renderer/` — React UI
- `tests/` — fake Claude Code CLI and scripted OpenRouter harness
- `C:\Users\prode\study-lab` — reference: app skeleton, `src/main/claude/*`, `src/main/harness/{model,agent,claude}.ts` (DeepAgents on ChatOpenRouter), `openrouter.ts`, `db.ts`, IPC
- `C:\Users\prode\MagnoTech\projeto-1-engenharia-autocad-csharp\desktop\electron` — reference: `turno.ts`, `leitorDoStream.ts`, `servidorDeRegras.ts`

## References

- `specs/app-shell/` — Electron skeleton, hardened window, validated IPC, safeStorage credential store with no plaintext fallback, delivery-gate commands
- `specs/event-log/` — unified event schema, secret redaction, SQLite index plus per-task raw JSONL, incremental push to the UI, crash recovery
- `specs/claude-specialist/` — executor for the pinned Claude Code CLI run in the sandbox container, subscription login on the sandbox config volume, stream-json parser with usage and cost, multi-turn stdin, kill and timeout
- `specs/orchestrator/` — DeepAgents (`createDeepAgent`) on `ChatOpenRouter` with a user-chosen model defaulting to `deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` with `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` as preset and fallback, `write_todos` decomposition, the specialist as a delegation tool fed a context package, `interruptOn` approval of writes, checkpointer for resume, consolidation, cancellation and recovery
- `specs/task-sandbox/` — one container per delegation with `workspace/<uuid>/` mounted at `/work`, prompt rendered only from the context package, egress proxy, audit of files touched, patch approval, discard ([adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task])
- https://reference.langchain.com/javascript/deepagents — orchestration framework
- https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/integrations/chat/openrouter — `ChatOpenRouter` from `@langchain/openrouter`: tool binding, streaming, `models` fallback routing, `provider.data_collection: "deny"` by default since source code is sent
- `specs/desktop-ui/` — settings, tasks and agents view, live logs, evidence and files, history, permissions, token and cost

## Out of scope

- Distributing the app to other users: the specialist authenticates with the user's own Claude plan login only, which is personal use
- Anthropic API key, Bedrock or Vertex authentication for the specialist
- OS-level isolation on the host: command execution, when enabled, runs only inside a container
- Analysis of software the user does not own or is not authorized to inspect

## Tasks

- [x] 1.1 (Unit) Write ADRs for DeepAgents on OpenRouter as the orchestration framework, the pinned Claude Code CLI over the Agent SDK for the specialist, subscription-login-only auth, the copy-in read-only sandbox with patch-gated writes, and SQLite plus JSONL event storage
- [x] 1.2 (Unit) Record the adopted stack in `docs/stack.md` and the canonical terms (orchestrator, specialist, delegation, context package, sandbox, evidence) in `docs/glossary.md`
- [x] 1.3 (Unit) Fill `.claude/rules/project.md` and record build, format, lint and test with `scc check set`
  _Depends 1.1, 1.2_
- [x] 2.1 (Unit) Record the orchestrator task container and the orchestrator-written
      brief as ADR 0007 and as deltas to specs/orchestrator and specs/task-sandbox
  _Reason The user asked mid-run for every agent tool to run in a sandbox and for the orchestrator to write the specialist's prompt_
- [x] 2.2 (Unit) Run the orchestrator's file and command tools in a per-task container
      with the source folder bind-mounted read-only, through a DeepAgents sandbox
      backend
  _Reason Same request: DeepAgents sees the whole workspace through a local bind, inside a sandbox_
- [x] 2.3 (Unit) Add the orchestrator-written brief to the context package, scrubbed of
      host paths, and render it first in the specialist's prompt
  _Reason Same request: the orchestrator writes the prompt and narrative handed to Claude Code with the prepared workspace_
- [x] 3.1 (Unit) Let the user choose the reasoning effort of the orchestrator and of the
      specialist in Settings
  _Reason The user asked mid-run to choose each model's effort_

## Done when

- `scc validate --checks --pr` exits 0 with every referenced spec's tasks ticked
- The end-to-end test runs a task through orchestrator, delegation, sandbox and consolidation against the fake Claude Code CLI and a scripted OpenRouter, and asserts the event log and the sandbox audit
- A real run on a sample repository shows the decomposition, the specialist's evidence and a proposed patch that is applied only after approval

```md
---
autonomy: auto

status: approved

---

# Projects and onboarding

A first-run setup that readies the sandbox, Claude Code and the orchestrator's model, then projects:
one target each, created through a guided setup, holding tasks that share its sandboxes, outputs and
analyses.

## Why

Today the desktop app opens on a bare request box: a task names a source folder, and nothing carries
from one task to the next on the same target. The user wants two changes:

- a first-run setup that readies the sandbox, signs Claude Code in on the user's own plan and
  configures an OpenAI-compatible model (OpenRouter by default) before anything else;
- projects created through an intuitive setup, in the spirit of rebuild tools such as craft-anything
  (see the wiki), each with its own UUID and workspace, and with the analyses of earlier tasks kept
  for the later ones.

## Paths

- `src/renderer/src/` — the setup flow, the project views, the sidebar, new shadcn/ui components
- `src/main/` — setup state, projects, project-scoped sandboxes and analyses, the runner
- `src/shared/` — the IPC contract and types
- `resources/` — the app icon and artwork, made with pixellab-cli

## References

- `specs/onboarding/` — the first-run setup: sandbox images, Claude Code sign-in, and the orchestrator's provider, key and model, with project creation locked until all three are ready
- `specs/projects/` — projects with a UUID and a folder, a guided setup (goal, target with its detected kind, model and effort), tasks inside a project sharing its sandboxes, outputs and analyses, and existing tasks moved into projects
- Delivered in order: specs/onboarding, then specs/projects
- adr:0010-build-the-renderer-on-shadcn-ui-and-radix
- adr:0017-keep-a-tasks-conversation-containers-and-files-until-it-is-deleted
- adr:0014-add-openai-compatible-orchestrator-providers

## Out of scope

- The terminal UI, which follows the same flow in a later plan
- Copying another app's wording, branding or artwork
- Sharing projects between machines or users

## Tasks

- [x] 1.1 (Unit) Make the app icon and the setup and project artwork with pixellab-cli, and wire the icon into the window and the installer
- [ ] 1.2 (Unit) Rebuild the task view as a chat timeline that tracks each agent's
      turns, tool calls and delegations in line, as Claude Code Web and Codex Web show a
      run
  _Reason The user asked for the run shown as a chat timeline, closer to Claude Code Web and Codex Web_

## Done when

# Specialist rea

The second round of the harness: sandbox images pulled from a registry, a specialist
container that never outlives its run, a chat that runs in English and can approve its
own tool calls, and a specialist built on REA with a sandbox free of all but its files, with the egress proxy gone.

## Why

Testing the first round showed a stale specialist image that the app took as ready, an
Anthropic usage-policy refusal with nothing done about it, prompts mixing the user's
language into the specialist's context, and a specialist without the reverse
engineering tools it needs. Done means the app prepares its images by itself at start,
cleans up every specialist container, handles a refusal once with what the user
states, runs every prompt in English, and lets the specialist analyse with REA and any
tool it installs, reaching only the files it was given.

## Paths

- `sandbox/` — the published base and the local specialist layer
- `.github/workflows/` — the image publishing workflow
- `src/main/sandbox/`, `src/main/status.ts`, `src/main/delegation.ts` — images, containers, delegation
- `src/main/orchestrator/` — prompts, gated tools, the context package
- `src/renderer/src/views/Settings.tsx` — image state, automatic tool calls
- https://github.com/morluto/rea — REA, the reverse engineering MCP server and skill

## References

- `specs/sandbox-images/` — a public base image on GHCR pinned by digest, the verified Claude Code CLI added in a local layer, automatic preparation at start, stale image detection, the egress proxy and its network removed, and both sandboxes given full internet access
- `specs/specialist-lifecycle/` — the specialist container removed whenever Claude Code ends, a usage-policy refusal as its own failure answered by one re-delegation per refused step with the purpose and authorization the user states, the specialist pinned to Opus 5.5
- `specs/chat/` — delta: an option per task to run every gated tool call, `apply_patch` included, without asking; every prompt, brief and context package in English, while the chat answers in the user's language
- `specs/rea-native/` — REA's MCP server, prompt and skill in the specialist, its shell and root inside its container with a writable root filesystem to install any tool — never `--privileged` nor the Docker socket — isolated only by the files it receives, the shared login volume kept with its exposure accepted, under its own ADR
- `specs/task-sandbox/`, `specs/orchestrator/`, `specs/desktop-ui/`, `specs/claude-specialist/` — deltas for the network, the image check, Settings and the model pin, each in the PR of the spec that changes it
- Delivered in order: specs/sandbox-images, specs/specialist-lifecycle, specs/rea-native, then the specs/chat delta
- adr:0012-pull-the-specialists-base-image-from-ghcr
- adr:0013-give-the-sandboxes-full-internet-access
- adr:0002-run-the-specialist-through-the-pinned-claude-code-cli
- adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task

## Out of scope

- Rewording a refused request automatically until the usage-policy check lets it through
- Publishing an image that holds the Claude Code binary
- Images for any platform but linux/amd64
- Restricting either sandbox's internet access
- Distributing the app to other users

# TUI revamp

A terminal UI for Harness for REA that works like the harness TUIs engineers already use — Claude Code
and OpenCode — and does everything the desktop app does: it opens on the folder it is run in, sets
itself up there, and shows each task as a live, readable conversation. Rebuilt on OpenTUI's React
layer over the core both apps share, with the data folder shared between any number of processes.

## Why

The 0.1 TUI is a thin imperative prototype: it ignores the folder it is started in, its one input line
and plain-text body make tasks hard to follow, several screens behave unexpectedly, and it lacks most of
what the desktop app offers (setup flow, settings, delegations, usage, event log, patches, decisions).
Its data-folder lock also lets only one app run at a time. Done means `harness-for-rea` run in any
folder opens that folder as a project, several terminals and the desktop app run side by side on one
data folder, and a task in the TUI can be started, followed, steered and reviewed with the same
information and actions the desktop app offers, through the interactions of Claude Code and OpenCode:
a status line, a multi-line prompt with history, slash commands and a command palette, file mentions,
collapsible tool calls, markdown and syntax-highlighted code, diffs, and dialogs for questions.

## Paths

- `tui/` — the TUI, rebuilt on `@opentui/react`; its npm package, `tui/src/paths.ts` flags and binary build
- `src/main/core.ts`, `src/main/lock.ts`, `src/main/db.ts`, `src/main/events/log.ts`, `src/main/projects.ts`, `src/main/status.ts`, `src/main/credentials.ts`, `src/main/sandbox/taskbox.ts`, `src/main/sandbox/specialistbox.ts` — sharing the data folder between processes
- `src/renderer/src/lib/` — the pure view logic both UIs reuse (timeline, chat, store, virtual window, format)
- `src/renderer/src/` views — the desktop side of the per-project lock and of cross-process refresh
- `src/shared/api.ts`, `src/shared/types.ts` — the refusal of a busy project, and anything the TUI needs that the API does not expose
- `scripts/test-gate.mjs`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `scripts/build-cli.ts`, `README.md`, `docs/adr/`, `docs/stack.md`
- `tests/lock.test.ts`, `tests/bun-core.test.ts` — assert the folder-wide lock and are rewritten with it

## References

- `specs/shared-data-folder/` — several processes on one data folder, under task 1.3's ADR: a lock per project held while a task of it starts or runs (the desktop app browses freely and shows a busy project as taken by the other app); tasks owned by a process identified by pid and start time, so start-up recovery and both container sweeps touch only tasks and containers of a process that is gone; SQLite with a busy timeout, migrations run once under a lock, and a database newer than the app refused naming the newer app; the first-start upgrade, the image build and the Claude sign-in done once across processes; the Electron single-instance lock kept; provider keys in one OS-keychain store both apps read; each app noticing changes another process made and refreshing within a stated latency
- `specs/tui-shell/` — the TUI's shell on `@opentui/react`: a layout of status line, transcript, prompt and a toggled sidebar; theme tokens matching the desktop app's dark and light themes; one keybinding system with a help overlay (`?`); slash commands with autocompletion and a command palette (Ctrl+P) over the same commands; dialogs, overlays and toasts; Esc to interrupt and Ctrl+C twice to quit; screen tests on OpenTUI's test renderer with simulated keys
- `specs/tui-launch/` — the folder it is run in as the project's target: `harness-for-rea [path]` opens the project whose target is that folder, lists them to pick from when there are several, or offers to create one prefilled (name from the folder, detected kind, goal, the Settings model); a home folder, a drive root, Downloads or a folder holding the app's data asks for the path to be typed to confirm before it is mounted, and the data folder itself is refused; the first-run setup runs inline when not completed; `--continue` reopens the folder's last task and `--resume` lists its tasks; `/projects` reaches every project
- `specs/tui-conversation/` — a task as a conversation at parity with the desktop timeline: agent messages as markdown with highlighted code, tool calls one line each and expandable, delegations with their context package, report, evidence, files copied, read and written, and the specialist's run, patches as diffs with their approve and reject decision, gated tool calls approved, edited or rejected, questions and the safeguard-refusal choice as selection dialogs, a working indicator with elapsed time, tokens and cost, stop, continue, close, cancel, start over and delete, older pages on scroll-up; a multi-line prompt with history, `@` file mentions completed from the project's target, and messages queued while a turn runs
- `specs/tui-panels/` — the desktop app's panels in the terminal: a sidebar with the plan, delegations, usage per agent and files touched; the event log with its agent filter; the project overview with tasks, analyses, unknowns and deletion; the setup screens with the image build log, the Claude sign-in opening the browser, cancel and sign out, the provider with its base URL, key and a model picker, and the banner when a ready step stops being ready; a settings editor with efforts and timeouts that reopens the setup; the new-project dialog with target detection
- Delivered in order: specs/shared-data-folder, specs/tui-shell, specs/tui-launch, specs/tui-conversation, specs/tui-panels
- adr:0022-run-the-tui-on-bun-with-opentui
- adr:0017-keep-a-tasks-conversation-containers-and-files-until-it-is-deleted
- adr:0020-group-tasks-into-projects-that-share-their-analyses
- adr:0006-run-the-specialist-inside-a-container-per-task
- [OpenCode's TUI](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/tree/dev/packages/tui) on `@opentui/solid`, and Claude Code's on Ink — interaction references, never code to copy

## Out of scope

- Replacing or reducing the desktop app: both stay, on the same data
- A non-interactive mode (`-p "<request>"` printing the answer and exiting)
- Linux builds of the TUI, and mouse-first interaction beyond what OpenTUI gives
- Copying another harness's code, wording, themes or branding

`sandbox/cheat-engine/hfr-bridge.lua`:

```lua
-- ============================================================================
-- HARNESS FOR REA — CHEAT ENGINE BRIDGE (read-only)
-- ============================================================================
-- Derived from miscusi-peek/cheatengine-mcp-bridge, MCP_Server/ce_mcp_bridge.lua at commit
-- 6bd7ce90479250a9b4b75e7944df9c105ecb2572 (2026-08-14), under the MIT licence below.
--
-- It answers only the commands that read: the process list, modules, memory regions, memory, value and
-- byte-pattern scans, pointer chains, disassembly, symbols and structures, plus ping, open_process and
-- get_opened_process_id, on its own pipe, \\.\pipe\hfr-cheat-engine. Every other upstream handler is
-- deleted, not disabled; any other method gets -32601 (specs/cheat-engine R2.1–R2.3,
-- adr:0026-proxy-host-engines-to-the-agents-as-mcp-integrations). tests/cheatengine.test.ts holds the
-- handler table equal to the app's catalog.
--
-- Install: copy this file into Cheat Engine's autorun folder and restart Cheat Engine.
--
-- MIT License
--
-- Copyright (c) 2025 miscusi-peek
--
-- Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy
-- of this software and associated documentation files (the "Software"), to deal
-- in the Software without restriction, including without limitation the rights
-- to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell
-- copies of the Software, and to permit persons to whom the Software is

-- The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all
-- copies or substantial portions of the Software.
--
-- THE SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED "AS IS", WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, EXPRESS OR
-- IMPLIED, INCLUDING BUT NOT LIMITED TO THE WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY,
-- FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE AND NONINFRINGEMENT. IN NO EVENT SHALL THE
-- AUTHORS OR COPYRIGHT HOLDERS BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM, DAMAGES OR OTHER
